modules.title: How Markets Work

objectives.text: Explain what an exchange, broker, clearing house and registry each do
Read a bid/ask quote and calculate spread cost
Distinguish market, limit and stop orders and when each can fail
Describe settlement cycles and why they matter

lessons.title: Who is in the market
lessons.body:
A trade passes through several parties. The investor sends an order to a broker. The broker routes it to an exchange (e.g. ASX, LSE, NYSE, SGX) or another trading venue, where it is matched against an opposite order. After the match, a clearing house (central counterparty) stands between buyer and seller so neither carries the other's default risk. Settlement then moves cash and securities; a registry or depository records the new owner. Market makers and other liquidity providers post buy and sell quotes continuously and earn the spread in exchange for carrying inventory risk. Regulators (ASIC in Australia, the SEC in the US, the FCA in the UK, MAS in Singapore) set conduct and disclosure rules. Knowing the chain tells you where costs, delays and failures can appear.

Why it matters: when something goes wrong, the failure sits in a specific part of this chain (broker routing, matching, clearing, settlement, or registry). Knowing who does what tells you whom to ask and which delay is normal.

Decision exercise: map one paper share trade from your intention to a settled owner of record. Name the broker, venue, clearer and registry in general terms. Then write one sentence on a cost or delay that could appear at each step.

Common errors: treating the last traded price as a promise of your fill; assuming the broker is the exchange; and forgetting that paper fills in this app never reach a real venue.

lessons.title: Quotes, spread and depth
lessons.body:
Every quote has a bid (highest price a buyer will pay) and an ask or offer (lowest price a seller will accept). The difference is the spread. Worked example (fictional): ABC Ltd quotes bid A$10.00, ask A$10.04. Spread = A$0.04. Mid-price = (10.00+10.04)/2 = A$10.02. Buying 1,000 shares at the ask and immediately selling at the bid loses 1,000 x 0.04 = A$40 before brokerage; that is a round-trip spread cost of 0.04/10.02 = about 0.40%. Depth is how many shares sit at each price level. A tight spread with thin depth can still be expensive for a large order, because the order 'walks the book' to worse prices.

Why it matters: the spread is the first, most reliable trading cost. If you ignore it, every backtest is too optimistic.

Decision exercise: a quote is bid A$3.40 / ask A$3.48 with 400 shares on the offer. You need 2,000 shares immediately. Mid is A$3.44, but a market buy will walk beyond A$3.48 if deeper book is worse. Write whether you would use a limit, split the order, or skip the name.

Common errors: quoting spread in cents without converting to percent of price; looking only at the top of book; and treating a one-share top-of-book print as evidence the stock is liquid.

lessons.title: Order types
lessons.body:
A market order executes immediately at the best available prices; it guarantees execution (in a normal market) but not price. A limit order sets the worst price you accept; it guarantees price but not execution. A stop (stop-loss) order becomes a market order once a trigger price trades; in a fast fall or an overnight gap it can fill well below the trigger. A stop-limit becomes a limit order at the trigger and may not fill at all. Time-in-force settings (day, good-till-cancelled, immediate-or-cancel) control how long an order lives. Example (fictional): you place a stop at A$9.50 on XYZ; the stock closes at A$9.80 and opens at A$9.10 after bad news. The stop triggers at the open and fills near A$9.10, not A$9.50.

Why it matters: order type is how you express a trade-off between price certainty and execution certainty. There is no type that gives both in a stressed market.

Decision exercise: you are willing to own ABC only at A$10.00 or better, and you do not want a fill at A$10.30 if the market runs. That is a limit order, not a market order. If you instead need to exit a leveraged position immediately, a marketable order may be the lesser evil, but you must accept price uncertainty, including a gap through any stop.

Common errors: using stop-market orders in thin names as if they were guaranteed exits at the trigger; leaving GTC limits active into earnings; and confusing a stop-limit (which may never fill) with a stop-market (which may fill far away).

lessons.title: Sessions, auctions and settlement
lessons.body:
Many exchanges open and close with an auction, where orders accumulate and a single price is struck that maximises matched volume. Continuous trading happens between auctions. Trading halts and price limits pause markets on news or extreme moves. Settlement cycles differ by market and change over time. As of 7 Nov 2026, ASX states that CHESS settles Australian cash-equity trades two business days after the trade (T+2), using delivery versus payment; ASX is consulting on a possible move to T+1 but has set no date. In the US, most securities moved to T+1 (one business day) from 28 May 2024, per the SEC's Investor.gov bulletin. Always check the venue's current rule. Settlement matters because unsettled funds may not be withdrawable, and selling shares you do not yet own creates fail risk. In the Transparent Trading app all trades are paper simulations: no real order reaches any venue.

Why sessions and time zones belong in market mechanics, not only in later data-quality notes. The same calendar date is not the same information set in Sydney, London and New York. An Australian cash-market decision made at 10:15 Sydney time cannot honestly use a New York close from later that same date. Store timestamps with an explicit zone and convert before asking what was known.

Auctions concentrate orders and can print far from the prior close, especially after news or at the open after a gap. Settlement then determines when cash and title move. As this lesson already notes, ASX cash equities were T+2 as of 7 Nov 2026 with T+1 under consideration, and most US securities moved to T+1 from 28 May 2024. Always re-check the venue.

Decision exercise: pick one ASX name and one US name and write, for a Tuesday trade, the weekday on which settlement would occur under the cycles taught here, skipping a mid-week public holiday in one market as a thought experiment.

Common errors: treating session times as interchangeable; ignoring auctions; and spending unsettled sale proceeds as if they were cleared cash.

lessons.title: Venues, fragmentation and fees
lessons.body:
Shares may trade on several venues, including alternative venues and dark pools that do not display orders. Best-execution rules require brokers to seek good outcomes, but your actual cost is: spread + brokerage + any exchange/clearing fees + market impact. Example (fictional): buy A$5,000 of shares, brokerage A$9.50 each way, spread 0.20% round trip. Total round-trip cost = 9.50x2 + 0.002x5,000 = 19 + 10 = A$29, or 0.58% of the position. A trade must earn more than this just to break even.

Why it matters: fragmentation means the price you see on one screen may not be the price you can hit in size.

Decision exercise: using the fictional A$29 round-trip cost on a A$5,000 position (0.58%), calculate how large a subsequent gain you need just to break even after a matching exit cost if you already paid the entry half. If the idea's expected edge is smaller than total round-trip cost, it is not a trade.

Common errors: comparing brokers only on headline commission; forgetting exchange or FX conversion fees on foreign names; and assuming paper mid-price fills will be available live.

lessons.title: Deep dive: the life of an order, practice case and common errors
lessons.body:
Follow one fictional paper order end to end. 09:58 Sydney: you enter a limit buy for 2,000 ABC at A$10.02 while the quote is A$10.00/A$10.04 with 1,500 shares offered at A$10.04. Your order rests in the queue at A$10.02 and becomes the new best bid. Price priority comes first, then time priority, so later bids at A$10.02 queue behind you. At 10:03 a seller hits your bid: 1,200 shares fill at A$10.02 and 800 remain. At 10:30 you cancel the rest. Result: a partial fill. The unfilled 800 shares are opportunity cost, which is real but invisible in P&L. Measure it against arrival price: if ABC closes at A$10.40, the missed 800 shares cost A$(10.40-10.02) x 800 = A$304 of foregone gain. That is a process consideration, not a 'loss'. Practice case: a thinly traded small cap quotes A$1.50/A$1.60 with 300 shares offered. A market buy for 5,000 shares could walk through several levels and average far above A$1.60. Correct approach: use a limit, size to visible depth, or skip the trade. Common errors: confusing last-traded price with the executable price; placing stops at round numbers where many others sit; forgetting that auctions can open far from the prior close; assuming paper fills equal live fills. Paper engines often fill at mid or at quotes without queue position or impact, so add a realistic slippage assumption. Limitations: venue rules, tick sizes, auction times and order types differ by exchange and broker. Check the venue's current rules before relying on any feature.

Queue-position note: this course does not give you auction-imbalance data or a full queue model to practise on, and paper engines usually ignore time priority. You should still understand the idea: at a given price, earlier orders typically fill first, so joining a long queue at a popular limit can leave you unfilled while the price moves away. Measure that as opportunity cost, not as a hidden loss in P&L.

If displayed depth is smaller than your order, do not assume the next levels are as generous as the first. Size to what you can see or use a limit.

modules.title: Shares, ETFs and Indices

objectives.text: Explain what a share represents and the rights attached
Compare ETFs, managed funds and individual shares
Understand how cap-weighted and equal-weighted indices are built
Calculate index weights and the effect of a constituent move

lessons.title: What a share is
lessons.body:
A share (stock, equity) is a fractional ownership claim on a company's residual value after creditors. Ordinary shareholders typically get voting rights and any dividends declared, and rank last in liquidation. Preference shares usually have a fixed dividend and rank above ordinary shares. Corporate actions change share counts without changing company value: a 2-for-1 split doubles shares and halves price; a rights issue offers new shares, often at a discount, diluting those who do not take up. Example (fictional): you own 300 shares at A$12. A 3-for-1 split gives 900 shares at about A$4. Value stays A$3,600 before market moves.

Why it matters: a share is a residual claim. That is why equity can go to zero after creditors are paid, and why dilution and splits change share count without automatically changing your economic percentage if you participate equally.

Decision exercise: you own 1% of a fictional company. It issues new shares equal to 25% of the existing count and you do not take up your rights. Your ownership becomes 1 / 1.25 = 0.8%. Write that outcome in one sentence before you discuss whether the issue price was attractive.

Common errors: treating a split as a gain or loss; ignoring that unpaid rights expire; and ranking ordinary shares above lenders in a failure.

lessons.title: ETFs and funds
lessons.body:
An exchange-traded fund holds a basket (an index, sector, bonds, commodities) and trades on an exchange like a share. Key checks: management expense ratio (MER), tracking difference against its index, spread, size, replication method (physically backed, or synthetic via derivatives; Moneysmart notes synthetic ETFs carry the extra risk that the derivative counterparty could fail), and domicile (which affects withholding tax). Example: a fund with 0.20% MER on A$10,000 costs about A$20 per year in fees, deducted inside the fund price. The SEC's investor bulletin (updated 29 Aug 2023) says most leveraged and inverse ETFs 'reset' daily and are designed to meet their objectives on a daily basis, so performance over weeks, months or years can differ significantly from the stated multiple, especially in volatile markets. SEC example: an index falls 10% and then rises 10%, ending -1%, while a 2x fund ends -4%.

Why it matters: an ETF is a package of rules, fees and counterparties, not a magic version of the index.

Decision exercise: two funds track similar exposures. Fund A is physically backed with a 0.10% MER. Fund B is synthetic with a lower MER. Using Moneysmart's warning that synthetic ETFs carry extra counterparty risk, write which extra question you would ask about Fund B before comparing fees.

Limitations: daily-reset leveraged and inverse ETFs are designed around a daily objective. Multi-day results can diverge from the headline multiple, as in the SEC's -10% then +10% example where the index ends about -1% and a 2x fund ends about -4%.

lessons.title: How indices are built
lessons.body:
An index is a rule-based basket used as a benchmark. Many major indices are float-adjusted market-cap weighted (weight = constituent float-adjusted market cap / total); check each provider's methodology. S&P Dow Jones Indices describes the Dow Jones Industrial Average as price-weighted: weights depend only on constituent prices, and a divisor adjusts for splits, special dividends, rights issues and constituent changes. Nikkei describes the Nikkei 225 as a price-weighted index of 225 stocks in the Tokyo Stock Exchange Prime Market. In a price-weighted index, high-priced shares dominate. Equal-weighted versions give each member the same weight at rebalance. Total-return indices reinvest dividends; price indices do not, so long-run comparisons must use the same type.

Why it matters: you cannot interpret an index move unless you know what the index is designed to represent.

This course does not claim a single weighting method for every well-known index. DJIA and Nikkei 225 are described by their providers as price-weighted (see the evidence register). Many other major indices use some form of float-adjusted capitalisation weighting, but you should read the current methodology for the index you study rather than infer it from a neighbour. Equal-weight and total-return versions answer different questions.

Decision exercise: if a high-priced member dominates a price-weighted basket, a split that halves that price (with a divisor adjustment) changes its influence. Explain in one sentence why the index provider adjusts the divisor.

lessons.title: Index weight arithmetic
lessons.body:
Worked example (fictional 3-stock index): A cap A$60bn, B A$30bn, C A$10bn; total A$100bn. Weights 60%, 30%, 10%. If A rises 5% and others are flat, index change = 0.60 x 5% = 3.0%. If C rises 20% and others flat, index change = 0.10 x 20% = 2.0%. Concentration therefore means a few large members drive most index moves; that is a risk to understand, not a flaw to ignore.

Why it matters: concentration is a hidden active bet inside a passive basket.

Decision exercise: using the fictional 60/30/10 weights, estimate the index move if A falls 8% and B and C each rise 4%. Result: 0.60 x -8% + 0.30 x 4% + 0.10 x 4% = -4.8% + 1.2% + 0.4% = -3.2%. The large member still dominated.

Common error: calling a cap-weighted index diversified without checking top-10 weight.

lessons.title: Global listings and share classes
lessons.body:
Companies may list in several places (dual listings), issue depositary receipts (ADRs/GDRs), or have multiple share classes with different votes. Prices in different currencies must be FX-converted before comparing. Trading hours differ: Tokyo, Sydney, Hong Kong, London and New York sessions overlap only partially, so news may hit one listing first.

Why it matters: the same company can trade as different instruments, in different currencies, during different hours.

Decision exercise: a depositary receipt rises 2% while the home-market share is unchanged and the home currency strengthened 2% against the receipt currency. Before calling that an arbitrage, convert both prices to one currency and check whether they represent the same claim and the same number of underlying shares.

Common errors: comparing unconverted prices; ignoring dual-class voting differences; and treating an after-hours print in one venue as the official close in another.

lessons.title: Deep dive: choosing between an ETF, a basket and single shares; practice case
lessons.body:
Comparison framework, with fictional figures. Goal: broad Australian equity exposure for a A$20,000 paper allocation. Option A: a broad ASX ETF at 0.10% MER. Option B: five large single shares. Option C: an active ETF at 0.70%. Annual fee drag: A = A$20, C = A$140, B = A$0 in fees but brokerage on five purchases plus single-company risk. Concentration check: if the top two members of the index are 20% of it, option A still carries meaningful concentration. Read the fact sheet's top-10 weight. Tracking difference over three years tells you what the fees and frictions actually cost. Practice case: a 2x leveraged daily ETF over two days when the index moves +10% then -10%. Index: 1.10 x 0.90 = 0.99, so -1%. Leveraged fund: 1.20 x 0.80 = 0.96, so -4%, not -2%. This is volatility decay. Common errors: comparing a price index with a fund's total return; ignoring withholding tax from fund domicile; assuming an ETF's quoted price always equals its NAV (spreads widen in stress); treating 'complex' or synthetic ETFs as simple index trackers. Limitations: index methodologies change and providers publish rule books; read the current methodology for the index you study.

Decision reminder: choose the instrument that matches the risk you intend to take. A broad ETF can still be concentrated. A five-stock basket reduces some single-name risk and adds others. A leveraged daily ETF adds path-dependence. Write the intended risk first, then pick the wrapper.

modules.title: Returns, Compounding and Honest P&L

objectives.text: Calculate simple, total and annualised returns
Separate realised from unrealised P&L and include all costs
Understand why drawdowns need larger gains to recover
Report performance honestly with cashflows considered

lessons.title: Simple and total return
lessons.body:
Simple price return = (end price - start price)/start price. Total return adds income: (end - start + dividends)/start. Example (fictional): buy at A$50, receive A$2 dividend, sell at A$54. Price return = 4/50 = 8%. Total return = (4+2)/50 = 12%. Costs reduce both; with A$0.50 per share of round-trip costs, net total = 5.5/50 = 11%.

Why it matters: price return and total return answer different questions. Omitting income overstates how cheap an asset looked and understates what an owner received.

Decision exercise: buy A$20, receive A$0.80, sell A$19.60, costs A$0.10. Price return = -2.0%. Total return before costs = (-0.40 + 0.80) / 20 = +2.0%. Net total return = (0.40 - 0.10) / 20 = +1.5%. Report the net figure.

Common errors: mixing a price index with a total-return portfolio; forgetting special dividends; and using trade currency when your account is reported in another currency.

lessons.title: Compounding and annualising
lessons.body:
Returns compound multiplicatively. Two years of +10% gives 1.1 x 1.1 - 1 = 21%, not 20%. Annualised (CAGR) = (end/start)^(1/years) - 1. Example: A$10,000 grows to A$14,641 in 4 years: (1.4641)^(0.25) - 1 = 10.0% per year. Never annualise a few days of results; a 2% week does not mean a sustainable 180% year.

Why it matters: compounding is why a string of moderate gains or losses is not the same as adding the percentages.

Decision exercise: three months of +5%, -3% and +4%. Cumulative = 1.05 x 0.97 x 1.04 - 1 = 5.9%, not 6%. Annualising that 5.9% as if it were a sustainable yearly rate would be dishonest.

Never annualise a few days of results. A 2% week is not evidence of a 180% year.

lessons.title: Drawdowns and recovery
lessons.body:
Drawdown = fall from a peak. Recovery needs gain = 1/(1-loss) - 1. A 20% loss needs 25% to recover; 50% needs 100%; 80% needs 400%. Max drawdown is the largest peak-to-trough fall over a period. It tells you what holding the strategy would have felt like, which average returns hide.

Why it matters: drawdown is the path a human (or an AI risk rule) actually has to live through.

Recovery arithmetic is unforgiving: a 30% loss needs about 42.9% to recover (1/0.70 - 1). That is why risk caps exist. It is also why no published recovery percentage is a promise you will get the required gain.

Common error: quoting average return without the worst peak-to-trough decline in the same window.

lessons.title: Realised, unrealised and fees
lessons.body:
Realised P&L is locked in by closing; unrealised (mark-to-market) changes with price. Honest P&L includes brokerage, spreads, financing, FX conversion and borrow fees. Example: paper account A$100,000; realised +A$1,200, unrealised -A$900, costs A$150. Net change = 1,200 - 900 - 150 = A$150, i.e. +0.15%. Showing only the +A$1,200 would be misleading.

Why it matters: picking only closed winners is the simplest way to fake skill.

Decision exercise: list realised P&L, unrealised P&L and itemised costs for a fictional week, then refuse to quote any of those numbers alone as the headline.

Common errors: hiding financing on leveraged products; omitting FX conversion; and marking illiquid paper positions at last trade without noting uncertainty.

lessons.title: Cashflows and time-weighted returns
lessons.body:
Deposits and withdrawals distort simple account growth. If an account goes A$10,000 to A$15,000 because you deposited A$5,000, return is 0%, not 50%. Time-weighted return (TWR) chains sub-period returns between cashflows and measures the strategy; money-weighted return (IRR) reflects your timing of deposits. Example: period 1 A$10,000 to A$11,000 (+10%); deposit A$5,000 so A$16,000; period 2 to A$15,200 (-5%). TWR = 1.10 x 0.95 - 1 = 4.5%.

Why it matters: cashflows are not performance. TWR asks how the strategy did; IRR asks how your timing of deposits did. Honest reporting often needs both, labelled.

Decision exercise: start A$8,000, rise to A$8,800 (+10%), withdraw A$800, then fall to A$7,200. After the withdrawal the account was A$8,000, so the second period is 7,200/8,000 - 1 = -10%. TWR = 1.10 x 0.90 - 1 = -1.0%, even though the cash ending value is A$7,200 after a withdrawal.

lessons.title: Deep dive: building an honest performance statement; practice case
lessons.body:
An honest statement answers seven questions: period covered, starting capital, deposits and withdrawals, net return after every cost, time-weighted return, maximum drawdown with dates, and number of trades or exposure. Worked case (fictional paper account): start A$50,000 on 1 Jul; +A$2,500 by 30 Sep (+5.0%); deposit A$10,000 on 1 Oct, giving A$62,500; ends 31 Dec at A$60,000 (-4.0% for Q4). TWR = 1.05 x 0.96 - 1 = +0.8%. Simple 'ending minus starting' would wrongly show +A$10,000 (+20%). Peak equity was A$63,800 in October, trough A$58,700 in December: max drawdown = 5,100/63,800 = 8.0%. Costs were A$420, already inside the figures. The honest headline is '+0.8% TWR, 8.0% max drawdown, 46 paper trades, net of modelled costs, paper only'. Common errors: averaging percentage returns arithmetically across periods (use compounding); excluding open losing positions; quoting the best month; mixing paper and live results; annualising short samples; reporting gross figures. Limitations: paper costs are estimates; live slippage, partial fills and emotions differ.

Use the seven-question template as a grading artefact: if any answer is missing, the statement is incomplete even if the return looks attractive. Paper versus live must be labelled every time.

modules.title: Interest Rates, Central Banks and Bonds

objectives.text: Explain how central banks set policy rates and transmit them
Price a simple bond and relate price to yield
Use duration to estimate price sensitivity
Read a yield curve and credit spreads
Interpret credit spreads and expected credit loss

lessons.title: Policy rates
lessons.body:
Central banks such as the Reserve Bank of Australia (which sets a target for the cash rate, the interest rate on unsecured overnight loans between banks, and bounds it with a corridor: per the RBA explainer it pays 0.10 percentage points below target on Exchange Settlement balances and lends at 0.25 points above. Because reserves are abundant, the cash rate can trade near the corridor floor; the RBA is moving to an 'ample reserves' system), US Federal Reserve (fed funds target range), European Central Bank, Bank of England and Bank of Japan set a short-term policy rate to pursue mandates such as price stability and employment. They implement it through open-market operations, standing facilities and interest on reserves, and may use balance-sheet tools (quantitative easing/tightening). Higher policy rates usually raise borrowing costs, slow credit growth and can strengthen the currency, though the effect is lagged and uncertain.

Why it matters: policy rates change the discount rate and the cost of leverage throughout the financial system, but they do so with lags and with no guarantee about the next equity or FX move.

Decision exercise: read the latest decision page of one central bank (not a headline recap) and write: the target or range, the date, and one implementation detail the bank itself describes. For the RBA, that includes the cash-rate target and the corridor around Exchange Settlement balances described in this lesson.

Common errors: treating a 25 basis-point move as an immediate, one-for-one change in every mortgage or bond yield; and assuming every central bank uses the same corridor design.

lessons.title: Bond basics and pricing
lessons.body:
A bond pays coupons and returns face value at maturity. Price = present value of cashflows at the market yield. Example (fictional): 2-year A$100 face, 5% annual coupon, market yield 4%. Price = 5/1.04 + 105/1.04^2 = 4.808 + 97.078 = A$101.89. Because yield (4%) is below coupon (5%), the bond trades above par. Price and yield move inversely.

Why it matters: if you cannot explain why price and yield move inversely, you will misread bond-fund headlines after rate news.

Worked check: the 2-year 5% coupon at a 4% yield was priced at about A$101.89 because the coupons are richer than the market now requires. If the yield rose to 5%, the same bond would be worth par. The mark-to-market loss is the cost of that yield rise even if coupons keep being paid.

Common errors: calling a government bond risk-free in real terms (inflation still matters); and confusing current yield with yield to maturity.

lessons.title: Duration and convexity
lessons.body:
Modified duration estimates % price change for a 1-percentage-point yield change: dP/P ~ -Dmod x dy. Example: Dmod = 6, yields rise 0.50% gives about -3% price change. Longer maturity and lower coupon mean higher duration. Convexity makes the estimate less precise for large moves; for ordinary bonds actual price falls less and rises more than duration alone predicts.

Why the sign must stay attached: dP/P is approximately minus modified duration times the yield change. If duration is 6 and yields fall 0.50%, the estimate is +3%, not -3%. Getting the sign wrong reverses every hedging decision.

Duration rises with maturity and falls as coupons increase, which is why a long zero has more interest-rate sensitivity than a short high-coupon note. Convexity means the straight-line duration estimate is imperfect for large moves; for ordinary (option-free) bonds, prices rise more and fall less than the line predicts.

Decision exercise: duration 4.5, yields rise 0.20%. Approximate price change = -4.5 x 0.20% = -0.90%.

lessons.title: Yield curve
lessons.body:
The yield curve plots government yields against maturity. Normally upward sloping; an inverted curve (short yields above long) has historically preceded some recessions, but it is not a reliable timing tool. Steepening/flattening describes changes in the gap, e.g. 10-year minus 2-year spread. Real yields = nominal minus expected inflation; inflation-linked bonds show market-implied real yields.

Why it matters: the curve is a map of yields by maturity, not a crystal ball.

An inverted curve has preceded some recessions historically, but it is not a reliable timing tool and it is not a trade signal by itself. Steepening or flattening describes how the gap between two points changes.

Common error: treating one 2s10s observation as a complete macro view.

lessons.title: Credit and spreads
lessons.body:
Corporate bonds yield more than government bonds of similar maturity; the difference is the credit spread, compensating for default risk and lower liquidity. Ratings agencies grade issuers (investment grade vs high yield). Expected loss ~ probability of default x loss given default. Example: 2% annual PD and 60% LGD gives about 1.2% expected annual loss, so a spread of 1.0% would not cover it.

Why it matters: extra yield is compensation for something, usually default risk, uncertainty and lower liquidity. If the extra yield is smaller than a reasoned expected loss, it is not obviously generous.

Expected loss is approximately probability of default times loss given default. It is an estimate, not the actual loss that will occur.

Common errors: treating a rating as a guarantee; and ignoring that spreads can widen without any default if risk appetite falls.

lessons.title: Deep dive: pricing, duration and credit in one worked case
lessons.body:
Fictional 3-year A$100 bond, 4% annual coupon, yield 5%. Price = 4/1.05 + 4/1.05^2 + 104/1.05^3 = 3.810 + 3.628 + 89.840 = A$97.28, below par because coupon < yield. Macaulay duration = sum(t x PV) / price = (1x3.810 + 2x3.628 + 3x89.840)/97.28 = 280.586/97.28 = 2.884 years. Modified duration = 2.884/1.05 = 2.747. If yields rise 0.50%, estimated price change = -2.747 x 0.5% = -1.37%, about A$95.94. Repricing exactly at 5.5% gives about A$95.95, so the estimate is close for small moves. Credit case: a corporate bond yields 6.8% versus a 4.6% government bond of the same maturity, a spread of 2.2%. Expected annual loss with PD 2.5% and LGD 60% is 1.5%, leaving about 0.7% for liquidity risk, uncertainty and return. Common errors: thinking a bond 'can't lose' if held (inflation, default and opportunity cost remain); confusing coupon with yield; ignoring call features; assuming central bank moves pass through instantly to every rate. Limitations: policy frameworks and tools differ across central banks and change over time; read the current statement from the bank concerned.

Re-check of the worked duration case: Macaulay duration 2.884 years and modified duration 2.747 were recomputed independently in this review from the listed cashflows and match the lesson. Use that habit: when a number matters, recompute it once from the cashflows rather than trusting a remembered figure.

lessons.title: Pairs and quotes
lessons.body:
FX is quoted as base/quote. AUD/USD = 0.6500 means 1 AUD buys 0.65 USD. If AUD/USD rises, AUD strengthened. Inverse: USD/AUD = 1/0.65 = 1.5385. Crosses like EUR/AUD can be derived: EUR/USD 1.08 / AUD/USD 0.65 = EUR/AUD 1.6615. The BIS Triennial Survey (press release 30 Sep 2025) reported global FX trading of about US$9.6 trillion per day in April 2025, with the US dollar the most traded currency.

Why it matters: every FX figure is a ratio. Reverse the base and the quote and you must invert the number, not subtract it from one.

Decision exercise: AUD/USD 0.7100. USD/AUD = 1 / 0.7100 = about 1.4085. If EUR/USD is 1.0850, EUR/AUD = 1.0850 / 0.7100 = about 1.5282. Write both results before you look at a calculator app's rounding.

The BIS April 2025 turnover figure (about US$9.6 trillion a day) is context for how large and continuous the market is, not a reason to use more leverage.

lessons.title: Pips and P&L
lessons.body:
For most pairs a pip is 0.0001 (for JPY pairs 0.01). Example (fictional paper trade): buy 100,000 AUD/USD at 0.6500, sell at 0.6550 = 50 pips. P&L = 100,000 x 0.0050 = US$500, converted to A$ at 0.6550: about A$763. Spreads in FX are quoted in pips; a 1.2-pip spread on 100,000 units costs US$12.

Why it matters: pip value depends on the pair's quoting convention and on the notional.

Worked check of the lesson example: buying 100,000 AUD costs 65,000 USD at 0.6500 and sells for 65,500 USD at 0.6550, a USD 500 profit. Converting that USD 500 into AUD at 0.6550 gives 500 / 0.6550 = about A$763. The conversion step uses the quote as USD per AUD, so you divide USD by the rate.

Common errors: treating every pip as 0.0001 (JPY pairs usually use 0.01); forgetting to convert P&L into home currency; and quoting pip P&L on the wrong notional.

lessons.title: What moves currencies
lessons.body:
Drivers include interest-rate differentials and expectations, inflation, trade and current account balances, commodity prices (AUD and CAD are linked to commodities), risk appetite (safe havens such as JPY, CHF, USD often rise in stress), capital flows and intervention. Forward FX prices reflect interest differentials (covered interest parity): forward = spot x (1+i_quote)/(1+i_base). This is not a forecast of future spot.

Why it matters: a currency is a relative price of two economies' money. Many things move it, and none of them give a sure one-way bet.

Covered interest parity sets a no-arbitrage forward from spot and interest differentials. It is an accounting relationship for hedged interest, not a forecast that spot will travel to the forward. Trading as if the forward were a prediction is a category error.

Common errors: treating commodity-currency links as iron laws; and ignoring intervention or capital-flow surprises.

lessons.title: Currency in foreign investing
lessons.body:
An Australian buying US shares has two returns: the share in USD and USD/AUD. Return in A$ = (1+r_asset)(1+r_fx) - 1. Example: US share +10%, USD falls 5% vs AUD: 1.10 x 0.95 - 1 = 4.5% in A$. Hedged funds remove most currency effect at a cost or benefit tied to rate differentials.

Why it matters: an unhedged foreign asset is always two trades, the asset and the currency.

Worked check: asset +8%, foreign currency +5% versus home: home-currency return = 1.08 x 1.05 - 1 = 13.4%. If instead the foreign currency falls 5%, the result is 1.08 x 0.95 - 1 = 2.6%. The sign on the FX leg matters as much as the asset leg.

Decision exercise: state whether your paper US-share position is intended to include USD exposure. If not, you need a hedge and you must account for its cost or benefit.

lessons.title: Leverage and carry in FX
lessons.body:
Retail FX is often traded with margin; small moves produce large P&L. Carry trade: borrow low-yield currency, hold high-yield one; earns the differential but suffers sharp losses when risk appetite collapses. Many regulators (e.g. ASIC, ESMA) restrict retail leverage on CFDs and require negative-balance protection. This app is paper-only.

Why it matters: FX moves look small in pips and large once levered.

A carry trade earns a differential only while the high-yielder does not fall enough to erase it. Those falls often arrive quickly when risk appetite drops. Regulatory leverage caps on retail CFDs exist because unconstrained gearing turns ordinary moves into account-ending ones. This app remains paper-only.

Common error: choosing the maximum allowed leverage because it is allowed.

lessons.title: Deep dive: FX exposure audit and practice case
lessons.body:
Audit a fictional paper portfolio of A$100,000: 40% Australian shares, 35% US shares (unhedged), 15% Japanese shares (hedged), 10% cash A$. Unhedged foreign exposure = 35%. If USD falls 8% against AUD, the FX hit is 0.35 x -8% = -2.8% of the portfolio before any share move. The hedged Japanese holding removes most yen effect; the hedge cost or benefit is roughly the AUD-JPY interest differential. Pip case: sell 50,000 EUR/USD at 1.0850 and buy back at 1.0815. Gain = 35 pips x 50,000 x 0.0001 = US$175. Convert at an AUD/USD of 0.66: about A$265. Common errors: forgetting to convert P&L into home currency; treating forward points as a forecast; using maximum leverage because the margin requirement allows it; ignoring weekend gap risk. FX trades around the clock on weekdays, but liquidity thins between sessions and around holidays. Limitations: retail FX/CFD rules differ by jurisdiction; check your regulator.

Home-currency audit reminder: list each position's currency, whether it is hedged, and the approximate portfolio weight. Multiply unhedged weight by a plausible FX shock (the lesson used -8% on a 35% USD weight for a -2.8% portfolio hit) and ask whether that shock is inside your risk budget. If not, reduce weight or hedge in the paper plan.

modules.title: Commodities

objectives.text: Classify energy, metals and agricultural commodities and their drivers
Explain futures curves, contango and backwardation
Calculate roll yield effects on commodity funds
Link commodities to producer equities and currencies

lessons.title: Commodity groups
lessons.body:
Energy (crude oil benchmarks such as Brent and WTI, natural gas, LNG, coal), industrial metals (copper, aluminium, nickel, iron ore), precious metals (gold, silver) and agriculture (wheat, soybeans, sugar, coffee) each respond to different supply and demand forces: OPEC+ policy and inventories for oil; Chinese construction and steel output for iron ore; weather and planting for grains; real rates and central-bank buying for gold.

Why it matters: calling something a commodity is not analysis. Oil, copper, wheat and gold respond to different inventories, weather, policy and financial conditions.

Decision exercise: pick one name from each group (energy, industrial metal, precious metal, agriculture) and write a single primary driver and one free official or exchange data source you could check. Do not invent a forecast.

Common error: treating a one-week inventory surprise as a complete thesis.

lessons.title: Futures curves
lessons.body:
Most commodity exposure is via futures. Contango: later contracts priced above near ones (often when inventories are ample and storage costs apply). Backwardation: near contracts above later ones (tight supply). Example (fictional): front oil future A$100, next month A$102. A fund rolling monthly sells at 100 and buys at 102, roughly a 2% negative roll that month if prices stay unchanged.

Why it matters: most people meet commodities through futures, not sacks of grain. The shape of the curve is part of the return.

If the front contract is A$80 and the next is A$76, the curve is in backwardation. A fund rolling from 80 down to 76, if prices otherwise stayed put, would book a positive roll of about 5% that month (buy the cheaper later contract). The opposite, rolling from 50 into 51, is about a 2% negative roll. These are illustrations, not predictions that spot will stay still.

Common errors: mixing calendar spreads with a view on the entire commodity complex; and forgetting contract specifications (units, delivery, tick value).

lessons.title: Roll yield and fund returns
lessons.body:
Commodity fund return ~ spot change + roll yield + collateral interest - fees. Example: spot flat over a year, roll -1% per month (~-11.4% compounded: 0.99^12-1), collateral 4%, fee 0.5%. Approximate return = -11.4% + 4% - 0.5% = about -7.9%. This is why a commodity ETF can fall even when spot prices end flat.

Why it matters: a flat spot price can still produce a large negative (or positive) fund return through roll and fees.

Worked reminder: 0.99^12 - 1 is about -11.4% from a 1% monthly negative roll, before adding collateral income and subtracting fees. Quote the compounding, not 12 times 1%.

If you cannot separate spot, roll, collateral and fees, you cannot explain a commodity ETF's year.

lessons.title: Producers and currencies
lessons.body:
Miners and energy producers have operating leverage to prices: with costs of A$70 per unit and price A$100, margin is A$30; a 10% price rise to A$110 lifts margin 33% to A$40. Commodity exporters' currencies (AUD, CAD, NOK, BRL) often co-move with key exports. Physical delivery: futures can require delivery at expiry; retail paper practice should close or roll before expiry.

Why it matters: a producer equity is an operating business with costs, debt and hedges, not a clean units-of-commodity claim.

Operating leverage: cost A$70, price A$100, margin A$30. A 10% price rise to A$110 lifts margin by A$10, or about 33%. The same percentage price fall compresses the margin just as sharply.

Decision exercise: write whether your paper thesis is about the curve, the producer, or the exporter's currency. They are different bets.

lessons.title: Data you can study for free
lessons.body:
Government and agency sources publish inventories and outlooks (e.g. the US EIA weekly petroleum status report, Australia's Department of Industry Resources and Energy Quarterly, USDA WASDE). Exchanges publish contract specifications. Use these rather than paid feeds for study.

Why it matters: free official series beat paid rumours for study.

The EIA weekly petroleum status report is one documented example (see the evidence register). Treat weekly data as revisable and seasonal. Read the latest release notes rather than a screenshot of one table.

lessons.title: Deep dive: commodity fund vs producer equity; practice case
lessons.body:
Case (fictional): you expect oil to stay flat for a year but the curve is in steep contango, -1.5% per month on the roll. A futures fund would lose about 1-0.985^12 = 16.6% from roll before collateral income. A producer with A$55/bbl all-in costs at an A$80 oil price earns A$25/bbl regardless of the curve shape, but it carries company risks: operations, hedging policy, debt and sovereign risk. Neither is 'better'; they are different exposures. Second case: a gold miner's hedge book. If 30% of next year's output is sold forward at A$2,800 and spot rises to A$3,200, the unhedged 70% captures the rise and the hedged 30% does not. Common errors: assuming commodity ETFs track spot; ignoring contract expiry and delivery; reading one week of inventory data as a trend; forgetting currency (most commodities are priced in USD). Limitations: weekly agency data such as the EIA Weekly Petroleum Status Report are revised; seasonal patterns matter.

When comparing a futures fund with a producer, write two columns: what each wins if your price view is right, and what each can lose even if the price view is right (roll, hedge book, operational failure, currency). Neither column is a recommendation.

objectives.text: Describe how blockchains, consensus and stablecoins work
Identify custody and counterparty risk
Size positions for crypto volatility
Calculate perpetual funding costs and leverage liquidation
Recognise scam red flags and regulator warnings

lessons.title: What crypto-assets are
lessons.body:
A blockchain is a shared ledger maintained by a network that validates transactions (proof-of-work or proof-of-stake). Bitcoin is a fixed-supply-schedule asset; Ether powers smart contracts on Ethereum. Stablecoins aim to track a currency via reserves or algorithms and have failed when reserves or designs proved weak. Crypto trades 24/7 across many venues worldwide, so prices can differ by venue.

Why it matters: the label crypto covers very different claims, from a scarce network asset to a token that depends on a team's treasury.

Decision exercise: before any paper crypto position, write in one line what the token's holders actually have a claim on. If you cannot answer, size must be smaller, not larger.

Venue prices can differ. A print on one exchange is not automatically available on another.

lessons.title: Custody and counterparty risk
lessons.body:
Self-custody means you hold private keys; losing them loses the assets. Exchange custody means you rely on the exchange's solvency and controls; exchange failures have caused large customer losses. ASIC's Moneysmart says most crypto are high-risk investments whose value is very volatile, and that crypto scams are common because transactions are hard to recover and trace. Moneysmart also notes new Australian laws for digital asset platforms are due to commence 8 April 2027.

Why it matters: operational loss (lost keys, insolvent custodian, irrecoverable transfer) can dominate market loss.

Moneysmart's warning that most crypto-assets are high-risk and that scams are common because transfers are hard to reverse is a reason for process, not a reason to hide the topic. New Australian digital-asset platform laws noted as commencing 8 April 2027 should be checked for their current status; this course does not give legal advice.

Decision exercise: list where the keys would live in your paper scenario and what failure that choice introduces.

lessons.title: Volatility and sizing
lessons.body:
Crypto volatility is typically several times that of broad equity indices. Example: if annualised volatility is 70%, a rough one-day 1-standard-deviation move is 70%/sqrt(365) = about 3.7%. A A$5,000 paper position could swing about A$183 on an ordinary day and much more in stress. Size accordingly.

Why it matters: higher volatility requires smaller notional for the same money risk.

Worked check: annualised volatility 70% and daily root using 365 gives about 3.7% for a one-standard-deviation day. That is a sizing input, not a promise that the next day will be that large or that small. Stress days can be several times larger.

lessons.title: Perpetual futures and funding
lessons.body:
Perpetual swaps have no expiry; a funding rate paid between longs and shorts keeps price near spot. Example: funding +0.01% every 8 hours on A$10,000 long = A$1 per period, A$3 per day, about A$1,095 per year (10.95%) if unchanged. High leverage on perpetuals leads to liquidation on small moves: at 20x, a ~5% adverse move wipes margin.

Why it matters: perpetual swaps embed a running payment and a liquidation engine.

Worked check: +0.01% each 8 hours is 0.03% a day, about 11% a year if unchanged. High positive funding on a long is a cost that a backtest must include. At 20x, a 5% adverse move exhausts margin if there is no buffer: 1 / 20 = 5%.

Common error: treating funding as optional colour rather than P&L.

lessons.title: Scams and red flags
lessons.body:
Guaranteed returns, pressure to move quickly, requests to send crypto to 'unlock' withdrawals, fake celebrity endorsements, and unsolicited 'account managers' are classic scam signs. Smart contracts can contain bugs; 'rug pulls' drain liquidity. Verify official sources; never share seed phrases.

Why it matters: guaranteed-return language is a warning sign, not a feature.

Decision exercise: rewrite any marketing sentence that promises a fixed daily coin yield as a journal entry titled unverified claim, then refuse to size it until a primary source exists. There will not be one for a guaranteed 2% a day.

lessons.title: Deep dive: crypto risk checklist and practice case
lessons.body:
Before any paper crypto position, answer: (1) Where is custody, and who holds the keys? (2) Which venue, and what are its jurisdiction and protections? (3) What is the 30-day realised volatility? (4) Is this a spot position, a perpetual with funding, or a token with unlock schedules? (5) What is the liquidity at your size? Case (fictional): a A$40,000 paper account with a 1% risk budget (A$400). Coin volatility is 80% a year, so daily about 80/sqrt(365) = 4.19%. A 3-sigma day is about 12.6%. Max position = 400/0.1256 = about A$3,180. Funding case: holding a A$10,000 perpetual long at +0.03% per 8h for 30 days costs 10,000 x 0.0003 x 3 x 30 = A$270, which is 2.7% of notional. Common errors: using 7-day vol from a quiet week; ignoring funding; keeping large balances on an exchange; trusting 'stable' tokens without reserve reports; clicking links in direct messages. Limitations: regulation is changing (e.g. Australia's digital asset platform laws due April 2027 per Moneysmart); check the current position.

The A$3,180 max-position example (A$400 risk, about 12.6% three-sigma daily move at 80% annualised volatility using 365) was recomputed independently in this review: 80 / sqrt(365) is about 4.19%, times 3 is about 12.56%, and 400 / 0.1256 is about A$3,185. Use the same method with your own volatility assumption and write the assumption down.

objectives.text: Explain futures, options, CFDs and swaps
Calculate option payoffs and breakevens
Quantify leverage, margin and liquidation
Explain basic option Greeks
Evaluate the cost of hedging and swaps

lessons.title: Futures and forwards
lessons.body:
A future is a standardised exchange-traded agreement to buy/sell at a set price later, margined daily (mark-to-market). A forward is a private, customised version. Example (fictional): an index future multiplier A$25 per point, index 7,800: notional = A$195,000. Initial margin 6% = A$11,700. A 1% fall (78 points) loses A$1,950, about 17% of margin.

Why it matters: futures quantity is notional, not margin. Mixing them up explodes apparent returns and hides risk.

Worked quantity check: multiplier A$25 per index point and index 7,800 gives notional = 25 x 7,800 = A$195,000. A 1% index fall is 78 points and A$1,950. If initial margin is 6% (A$11,700), that 1% index move is about 17% of margin. The loss is A$1,950, not 1% of A$11,700.

A forward is customised and typically not exchange-margined in the same way; counterparty risk then sits with the other party rather than a central clearer.

lessons.title: Options payoffs
lessons.body:
A call gives the right to buy at the strike; a put the right to sell. Buyer pays a premium; maximum loss = premium. Example: buy a A$50 call for A$2. At expiry: share A$56 profit = 56-50-2 = A$4; share A$51 = -A$1; below A$50 = -A$2. Breakeven = strike + premium = A$52. Put breakeven = strike - premium. Writing (selling) naked calls has theoretically unlimited loss.

Why it matters: payoff diagrams make the maximum loss and the breakeven visible before you argue about direction.

Call buyer breakeven = strike + premium. Put buyer breakeven = strike - premium. At expiry a long call on a share finishing below the strike loses the entire premium, not zero and not the strike.

Selling naked calls has theoretically unlimited loss. That is a sizing and permission issue, not a clever income idea.

lessons.title: Greeks
lessons.body:
Delta: option price change per A$1 underlying move (call 0 to 1, put -1 to 0). Gamma: change of delta. Theta: time decay, usually negative for buyers. Vega: sensitivity to implied volatility. Example: call delta 0.40, share +A$1.00 gives option ~ +A$0.40.

Why it matters: Greeks are local, model-based sensitivities. They change as the market moves.

Delta 0.40 means about A$0.40 of option-price change for a A$1 underlying move, nearby, not forever. Gamma describes how quickly that delta changes. Theta is the cost of waiting for a long option. Vega is sensitivity to implied volatility, which can fall even when you are right on direction.

Common error: treating a morning delta as still true after a large move.

lessons.title: CFDs and margin
lessons.body:
A contract for difference pays the price change on an underlying without ownership, financed overnight. Leverage = notional / margin. At 20:1, a 5% adverse move loses 100% of margin. In Australia, ASIC's CFD product intervention order (Instrument 2020-986) requires retail clients to post minimum initial margin of 3.33% of notional for major FX pairs (about 30:1), 5% for major indices, minor FX pairs and gold (20:1), 10% for minor indices and other commodities (10:1), 50% for crypto-assets (2:1) and 20% for other underlyings such as shares (5:1). It also requires margin close-out protection and negative balance protection. As of Nov 2026 ASIC is consulting (CS 64) on extending the order, currently due to expire 23 May 2027. Other jurisdictions set different rules.

Share-margin worked case (US investor-education example, not an Australian rule and not a recommendation). The SEC Office of Investor Education and Advocacy's Investor Bulletin Understanding Margin Accounts (10 June 2021), read in full from investor.gov, states that under Regulation T you may borrow up to 50 percent of the purchase price of margin securities (initial margin), that some firms require more, and that FINRA rules require a maintenance requirement of at least 25 percent of the total market value of the margin securities, while many firms set higher house requirements, typically 30 to 40 percent or more. The bulletin's own example: you buy US$16,000 of securities by borrowing US$8,000 and paying US$8,000. If market value falls to US$12,000, equity is US$12,000 - US$8,000 = US$4,000. At a 25 percent maintenance requirement you need 0.25 x 12,000 = US$3,000, so US$4,000 still meets it. At a 40 percent house requirement you need 0.40 x 12,000 = US$4,800. Equity is then US$800 short, and the firm may issue a margin call for that US$800. The same bulletin warns that you can lose more than you invested; the firm may sell securities without notice and without letting you choose which names; it may raise house requirements without advance notice; and you are not entitled to an extension of time.

Australian retail CFD margins remain the separate ASIC PIO minima already taught in this lesson (3.33% major FX, 5% major index / minor FX / gold, 10% minor index and other commodities, 50% crypto, 20% other such as shares), with close-out and negative-balance protection, and with the order's dated consultation status. Do not import US share-margin percentages into an Australian CFD account, or the reverse.

Leverage identity: at 20:1, notional / margin = 20, so a 5% adverse move on notional equals 100% of margin. That identity is arithmetic, not a forecast.

lessons.title: Swaps and hedging
lessons.body:
Interest-rate swaps exchange fixed for floating payments; total-return swaps pass an asset's return. Hedging reduces risk but costs carry or premium: e.g. buying a put for 3% of portfolio value per year caps downside below the strike but drags returns if markets rise.

Why it matters: a hedge is a second position with its own cost and basis risk, not an eraser.

Decision exercise: a protective put costing 3% of portfolio value per year caps downside below the strike and reduces returns by roughly that premium if markets rise. Write whether that cost is acceptable for the risk being reduced. If you cannot name the risk, it is not a hedge.

lessons.title: Deep dive: Greeks in a worked case, and leverage reality
lessons.body:
Fictional option: a 30-day call on XYZ, strike A$50, share A$50, premium A$2.00, delta 0.52, gamma 0.06, theta -A$0.04/day, vega A$0.08 per volatility point. Tomorrow the share is A$51 and implied vol is unchanged. Approximate change = delta x 1 + 0.5 x gamma x 1^2 + theta = 0.52 + 0.03 - 0.04 = +A$0.51, so the option is about A$2.51. If instead implied vol falls 5 points (as after an earnings announcement) with the share flat: 5 x -0.08 + theta -0.04 = -A$0.44. Buyers can lose even when right on direction if the vol crush outweighs the move. Leverage case: a A$5,000 margin on a 20:1 index CFD (A$100,000 notional). An adverse 3% move = -A$3,000 = -60% of margin; under ASIC's rules a retail account must be closed out once equity falls below the required close-out protection level. Common errors: selling options for 'income' without sizing tail risk; holding through expiry by accident; equating margin with risk; ignoring dividends and early-exercise features. Limitations: Greeks are model estimates that change continuously.

Greeks check: delta 0.52 + half gamma 0.03 + theta -0.04 = +0.51, matching the lesson's approximate next-day value of A$2.51 if the share rises A$1 with unchanged implied volatility. A five-point implied-vol fall at 0.08 vega per point, plus theta, is about -0.44 with the share unchanged. Direction can be right and the option still lose money.

Do not equate unused margin with unused risk.

modules.title: Liquidity, Execution and Trading Costs

Estimate slippage and market impact

Choose execution methods that reduce costs

lessons.title: Liquidity measures
lessons.body:
Liquidity is ability to trade size quickly near the current price. Measures: spread (bps), average daily volume (ADV), depth at top levels, and turnover. Rule of thumb: keep orders a small fraction of ADV; trading 10% of ADV in one go often moves price noticeably. Small caps, frontier markets, and off-hours crypto are often thin.

Why it matters: liquidity is about the size you can transact near the current price, not about whether a quote exists.

Decision exercise: your order is 8% of ADV. Using the lesson's rule of thumb that 10% of ADV in one go often moves price, write whether you will split, use a limit, or skip. Then record displayed depth at the first two levels if you can see them.

Common error: treating yesterday's ADV as a guarantee of today's depth, especially around news.

lessons.title: Slippage and impact
lessons.body:
Slippage = fill price minus decision (or arrival) price. Example: decide to buy at mid A$5.00, fill average A$5.03 on 10,000 shares: slippage = A$300 (0.6%). A common rough impact model: cost ~ k x volatility x sqrt(order size / ADV). It is an approximation, useful for comparing sizes, not exact prediction.

Why it matters: slippage is often larger than brokerage and is invisible if you only record last price.

Worked check: decision mid A$5.00, fill A$5.03, 10,000 shares, slippage = A$300 or 0.60%. The square-root impact sketch (k times volatility times sqrt(size/ADV)) is a comparison tool, not a precise forecast.

Paper engines that fill at mid hide this cost. Add an assumption rather than pretend it is zero.

lessons.title: Financing, borrow and FX costs
lessons.body:
Leveraged longs pay financing (e.g. benchmark + 3% annual on notional). Shorts pay borrow fees, which can spike for hard-to-borrow stocks, and must pay dividends to the lender. Example: A$20,000 short, borrow 2% annual for 30 days = 20,000 x 0.02 x 30/365 = A$32.88. Converting A$ to USD at a 0.5% FX margin costs A$50 per A$10,000 each way.

Why it matters: carry can turn a correct directional view into a net loss if you stay too long.

Worked check: A$20,000 short, 2% annual borrow, 30/365 days: 20,000 x 0.02 x 30/365 = about A$32.88, matching the lesson. Hard-to-borrow names can gap to much higher fees or be recalled.

FX conversion margins apply each way when you move between currencies.

lessons.title: Tax caveats
lessons.body:
Tax treatment depends on jurisdiction and personal circumstances: capital gains rules and holding-period discounts (example, Australia per ATO: an Australian-resident individual who owned an asset for at least 12 months, excluding the acquisition and disposal days, can generally reduce the capital gain by 50% after first subtracting capital losses; exclusions exist: foreign and temporary residents cannot use the full discount, and companies cannot use it. The ATO page, last updated 29 June 2026, also notes that CGT changes announced in the 2026-27 Federal Budget do not apply to Tax Time 2026, so check current rules), franking credits, withholding tax on foreign dividends, and trader vs investor classification. This course gives general information only; check official sources such as the ATO, HMRC or IRS, or a qualified adviser. Paper trades have no tax effect.

Tax remains general information only. The ATO CGT-discount description already in this lesson (including the foreign/temporary-resident exclusion, the 12-month rule excluding acquisition and CGT-event days, losses first, and the Budget 2026-27 caveat on the page dated 29 June 2026) should be re-checked on the official page before anyone relies on it. This course does not compute a learner's tax or give tax advice.

lessons.title: Execution choices
lessons.body:
Limit orders control price; splitting orders (TWAP/VWAP style) reduces impact; avoid illiquid open/close minutes unless using auctions deliberately; check news calendars. Measure your paper fills against arrival price so improvements are evidence-based.

Why it matters: execution choice is part of expected return.

Prefer limits when you can wait; respect auctions if you intend to participate in them; avoid becoming a large fraction of a thin book. Measure paper fills against arrival mid so that improvement is visible.

lessons.title: Deep dive: implementation shortfall worked case
lessons.body:
Fictional plan: buy 20,000 shares of DEF, decision mid A$4.00, ADV 400,000 (order = 5% of ADV). Executed over the day: 8,000 at A$4.01, 7,000 at A$4.03, 5,000 at A$4.05. Average = (32,080 + 28,210 + 20,250)/20,000 = A$4.027. Slippage = 0.027/4.00 = 67.5 bps = A$540. Brokerage A$40. FX not applicable. Total implementation cost about A$580 (0.73%). If the expected edge of the idea was 1.0%, costs consumed most of it. Short case: short 5,000 GHI at A$20 for 60 days, borrow 3% a year, A$0.30 dividend paid during the period. Borrow = 100,000 x 0.03 x 60/365 = A$493; dividend owed = A$1,500. Total carry A$1,993, about 2% of notional. Common errors: modelling backtests at mid prices; ignoring borrow recalls; forgetting FX conversion on foreign trades; assuming tax rules from one country apply elsewhere. Tax: general information only. Australian example from the ATO, the 12-month CGT discount for resident individuals; rules, rates and eligibility depend on jurisdiction and circumstances.

Implementation-shortfall check: average fill A$4.027 versus A$4.00 mid is 67.5 bps or A$540 on 20,000 shares, plus A$40 brokerage, about A$580 or 0.73%. If the idea only had 1% of expected edge, costs consumed most of it. That arithmetic is why mid-price backtests mislead.

modules.title: Reading Financial Statements

objectives.text: Read the income statement, balance sheet and cash flow statement
Link the three statements
Calculate margins, leverage and liquidity ratios
Spot earnings-quality warning signs

lessons.title: Income statement
lessons.body:
Revenue - cost of goods sold = gross profit; less operating expenses = operating profit (EBIT); less interest and tax = net profit. EBITDA adds back depreciation and amortisation but ignores capital spending needs. Example (fictional, A$m): revenue 500, COGS 300, opex 120, D&A 20 included in opex, interest 10, tax 21. Gross 200 (40%), EBIT 80 (16%), EBITDA 100, pre-tax 70, net 49 (9.8%).

Why it matters: margins tell you what is left after each layer of cost. Comparing companies without matching the layer (gross versus EBIT versus net) is a category error.

Worked check of the fictional figures: revenue 500, COGS 300, gross 200 (40%); after opex 120, EBIT 80 (16%); EBITDA 100 once D&A of 20 is added back; net 49 (9.8%). EBITDA is not cash and ignores capex.

Decision exercise: recompute each margin from a real annual report's numbers and write the page you took them from.

lessons.title: Balance sheet
lessons.body:
Assets = liabilities + equity. Current assets (cash, receivables, inventory) vs current liabilities (payables, short debt) gives the current ratio. Net debt = borrowings - cash. Example: current assets 150, current liabilities 100: current ratio 1.5. Debt 200, cash 50, EBITDA 100: net debt/EBITDA 1.5x.

Why it matters: solvency and liquidity live on the balance sheet, not only in the earnings headline.

Current ratio = current assets / current liabilities. Net debt = borrowings minus cash (definitions vary slightly by company; read the note). A low current ratio with large near-term debt is a different risk than a high net-debt/EBITDA funded by long maturities.

Common error: treating book equity as what shareholders would receive in a sale tomorrow.

lessons.title: Cash flow statement
lessons.body:
Operating cash flow (OCF), investing (capex, acquisitions), financing (debt, dividends, buybacks). Free cash flow (FCF) ~ OCF - capex. Profit and cash differ due to working capital and non-cash items. Example: net profit 49, D&A +20, receivables up 15 (cash tied up): OCF ~ 54. Capex 30: FCF 24.

Why it matters: profit can rise while the business consumes cash.

Worked reminder: net profit 49, add D&A 20, subtract a A$15 receivables increase, approximate OCF 54; subtract capex 30, FCF 24. If receivables keep growing faster than sales, ask whether earnings quality is deteriorating.

FCF definitions also vary (leases, interest, acquisitions). Write the definition you used.

lessons.title: Linking statements
lessons.body:
Net profit flows to retained earnings in equity; depreciation reduces asset values and is added back in OCF; capex adds to assets; debt raised appears in financing and liabilities. If profit consistently far exceeds OCF, investigate.

Why it matters: the three statements are one system. If they do not reconcile, you are missing a note or a classification.

Decision exercise: trace one year's net profit into retained earnings and one year's capex into the asset line, using a real report. If you cannot, you are not finished reading.

lessons.title: Quality red flags and standards
lessons.body:
Warning signs: receivables growing much faster than revenue, frequent 'one-off' adjustments, capitalising ordinary costs, rising inventory days, auditor changes, related-party deals. Most listed companies outside the US report under IFRS (Australia uses AASB, aligned with IFRS); US companies use US GAAP and file 10-K reports. Read notes, not just headlines.

Why it matters: quality problems often show up first as unusual relationships, not as a single shocking number.

Receivables growing much faster than revenue, recurring one-off adjustments, and auditor changes are prompts to read notes, not automatic proof of fraud. Standards differ (IFRS/AASB versus US GAAP). Compare like with like.

lessons.title: Deep dive: three-statement walk-through and red-flag drill
lessons.body:
Fictional company, year 2 versus year 1 (A$m): revenue 600 vs 520 (+15.4%); receivables 180 vs 110 (+63.6%); inventory 140 vs 120; net profit 60 vs 52; operating cash flow 18 vs 58; capex 40. FCF = 18 - 40 = -22. Receivable days rise from 110/520x365 = 77 to 180/600x365 = 110 days. Profit grew while cash flow collapsed. Ask whether revenue recognition got more aggressive, a big customer is paying late, or channel stuffing is occurring. Read the notes for revenue policy changes, customer concentration and factoring arrangements. Second drill: 'adjusted EBITDA' excludes A$35m of 'one-off' restructuring costs for the fourth year running. Recurring one-offs are operating costs. Common errors: valuing on EBITDA for capital-intensive firms; ignoring leases and off-balance-sheet obligations; comparing companies under different standards without adjustment; skipping the auditor's report. Sources: the SEC's Investor.gov guide says a 10-K gives a detailed picture of the business, its risks and its financial results, and management's discussion. In Australia, annual reports are lodged with ASX/ASIC.

Receivable-days check: 110/520 x 365 is about 77 days; 180/600 x 365 is about 110 days. Profit up, operating cash flow down, days up: the right response is a list of questions, not an immediate valuation slogan.

lessons.title: Multiples
lessons.body:
P/E = price / earnings per share. Enterprise value (EV) = market cap + net debt (+ minorities, preferred). EV/EBITDA compares businesses with different debt. P/B = price / book value per share, useful for banks and insurers. Example (fictional): price A$20, EPS A$1.60: P/E 12.5. Market cap A$2bn, net debt A$0.5bn, EBITDA A$0.25bn: EV/EBITDA 10x.

Why it matters: a multiple is a price divided by a base. If the base is peak-cycle, unusual, or not comparable, the multiple is decorative.

P/E uses equity value and earnings. EV/EBITDA uses enterprise value and a pre-interest base, so it is better for comparing firms with different debt, provided you compute EV consistently (market cap plus net debt and other claims). P/B is more useful where book value is meaningful, such as many banks, and less useful where book ignores the main assets.

Decision exercise: using the fictional P/E of 12.5 (A$20 / A$1.60) and EV/EBITDA of 10x, write one reason each multiple could be misleading (for example, one-off earnings, or capex ignored by EBITDA).

lessons.title: Yields
lessons.body:
Earnings yield = EPS/price (inverse of P/E). Dividend yield = DPS/price; in Australia franking credits may raise the grossed-up yield for eligible shareholders. For a fully franked dividend, grossed-up = cash yield / (1 - company tax rate used for franking). Per ATO guidance, the maximum franking credit depends on the payer's 'corporate tax rate for imputation purposes': 25% for base rate entities (from 2021-22) and 30% otherwise. This course's examples assume 30% for illustration only, and the result also depends on the franking percentage and the shareholder's circumstances: 4.2% fully franked / 0.7 = 6.0% grossed up. FCF yield = FCF / market cap.

Why it matters: yields look comparable only after you know whether income is cash, franked, or a one-off.

The franking example in this lesson uses a 30% illustrative company tax rate for imputation and notes that base-rate entities may use 25% from 2021-22 per the ATO page dated 9 December 2020. Check the current official page and the paying entity before using either rate. Grossed-up yield = cash yield / (1 - company tax rate used for franking) when the dividend is fully franked.

FCF yield = FCF / market cap (or sometimes equity FCF definitions). Write the FCF definition.

lessons.title: Discounted cash flow
lessons.body:
Value = sum of future FCF discounted at a required rate + terminal value. Gordon terminal value = FCF_next / (r - g). Example: FCF next year A$10m, r = 9%, g = 3%: TV = 10/0.06 = A$166.7m. Sensitivity: at r = 8%, 10/0.05 = A$200m. Small assumption changes move value a lot, so use ranges.

Why it matters: discounted cash flow turns assumptions into a number that looks more precise than it is.

Gordon terminal value = next FCF / (r - g) is undefined or explosive if g is close to r, and it is nonsense if g exceeds a reasoned long-run nominal growth rate for the economy. Sensitivity is the point of the exercise: the lesson's shift from r = 9% to r = 8% moved terminal value from A$166.7m to A$200m on the same A$10m FCF.

Decision exercise: refuse to publish a single point value. Publish a range and the assumptions that drive it.

lessons.title: Unit metrics
lessons.body:
Subscription: ARPU (average revenue per user), churn, CAC (customer acquisition cost), LTV ~ ARPU x gross margin / monthly churn. Example: ARPU A$30/month, margin 70%, churn 2%/month: LTV = 30 x 0.7 / 0.02 = A$1,050; CAC A$350 gives LTV/CAC 3.0. Retail: same-store sales, sales per square metre. Mining/energy: all-in sustaining cost (AISC) per ounce, cost per barrel. Airlines: RASK/CASK. Banks: net interest margin. Insurers: combined ratio.

Why it matters: unit metrics translate a business model into numbers you can compare, but companies define many of them differently.

Subscription LTV using ARPU x gross margin / monthly churn assumes a constant churn and margin forever. In the lesson, 30 x 0.70 / 0.02 = A$1,050. If monthly churn is actually 3%, LTV falls to A$700 and LTV/CAC at a A$350 CAC drops from 3.0 to 2.0. Always read the company's definition of ARPU, churn and CAC.

Other unit metrics taught later by sector (AISC, RASK/CASK, NIM, combined ratio, cap rate) have the same rule: write the definition before you compare two firms.

lessons.title: Valuation traps
lessons.body:
Cheap can be cheap for a reason: peak-cycle earnings make cyclicals look cheap at the top; one-off gains inflate EPS; heavy dilution erodes per-share value; high yields may precede dividend cuts. Compare to history and peers, and check cash conversion.

Why it matters: cheapness without a reason is often a warning.

Peak-cycle earnings, one-off gains, upcoming dilution and unsustainable dividends are standard traps. Compare with history and with peers, then check whether earnings turn into cash.

lessons.title: Deep dive: valuation range, not a point; practice case
lessons.body:
Fictional company: FCF next year A$50m, net debt A$200m, 100m shares. Scenario grid with Gordon value = FCF/(r-g). Base r 9%, g 3%: EV = A$833m, equity A$633m, A$6.33/share. Bear r 10%, g 2%: EV = A$625m, equity A$425m, A$4.25. Bull r 8%, g 3.5%: EV = A$1,111m, equity A$911m, A$9.11. The range of A$4.25 to A$9.11 shows how assumption-driven the result is; at a A$6.00 share price the conclusion is 'roughly fairly priced, wide uncertainty', not 'buy'. Sector unit metrics, with limitations: banks use P/B and ROE (book values depend on loan-loss assumptions); insurers use the combined ratio (reserves can be strengthened later); miners use AISC (definitions vary by company); software uses LTV/CAC (churn assumptions dominate); REITs use NTA discounts (valuations lag markets); airlines use RASK-CASK (fuel and FX swing it). Common errors: mixing equity multiples with EV measures; using a terminal growth rate above the long-run nominal economy; double-counting cash; ignoring dilution from options and convertibles.

The scenario grid (A$4.25 to A$9.11) is the product: a range plus uncertainty, not a buy call at A$6.00. If an AI tool outputs a single fair value without the grid, ask it for the r and g assumptions and recompute.
