objectives.text: Analyse bank profitability via NIM, cost-to-income and loan losses
Assess bank capital (CET1) and funding/liquidity
Relate the credit cycle to bank earnings
Analyse insurers via combined ratio, float and reserves
Analyse exchanges, payments and asset managers' fee economics

lessons.title: Bank economics
lessons.body:
Banks earn net interest income (loan yield minus funding cost). NIM = net interest income / average interest-earning assets. Example (fictional): NII A$18bn, average earning assets A$900bn: NIM 2.0%. Cost-to-income = operating costs / operating income; lower is more efficient. Impairment charges rise in downturns; loan loss rate = impairments / gross loans.

Why it matters: a bank's earnings are a spread business with a credit overlay.

NIM = net interest income / average interest-earning assets. The fictional 18 / 900 = 2.0% is a level, not a quality score, until you know mix (mortgages versus unsecured), hedging and how quickly deposits reprice. Cost-to-income shows efficiency; loan-loss rates show credit cost.

Decision exercise: if NIM widens 10 basis points on A$900bn of earning assets, that is about A$0.9bn of extra NII before losses. Ask what extra impairments might arrive later in the same rate cycle.

lessons.title: Capital and funding
lessons.body:
Basel III frameworks require minimum capital such as CET1 ratio = common equity tier 1 / risk-weighted assets; national regulators (APRA in Australia) set specific requirements. Funding mix (deposits vs wholesale) and liquidity metrics (LCR, NSFR) matter: rapid deposit flight has toppled banks. ROE = net profit / equity; high ROE from thin capital is riskier.

Why it matters: capital and funding are what keep a bank open when loans sour or deposits leave.

CET1 ratio = common equity tier 1 / risk-weighted assets is general Basel-style terminology used in this course as a reference. This review did not newly verify a specific APRA numerical minimum from primary text, so treat any number you see in a bank report as that bank's reported figure against its regulator's current rules, not as a universal legal minimum taught here. LCR and NSFR are likewise general names for liquidity and stable-funding metrics; read the regulator and the bank's disclosure rather than memorising an unverified threshold.

High ROE produced by thin capital is a risk statement, not a compliment.

lessons.title: Credit cycle
lessons.body:
Credit growth, lending standards, house prices and unemployment drive bank earnings. Rising rates can widen NIM initially but raise defaults later. Watch arrears data and regulator stress tests.

Why it matters: bank earnings are cyclical even when they look dull.

Credit growth, underwriting standards, house prices and unemployment tend to move together over a cycle. Rising rates can lift NIM first and lift defaults later. Watch arrears and published stress tests as process checks, not as guarantees of future losses.

Decision exercise: write one leading indicator you will record for a paper bank position (for example, 90-day arrears) and the change that would make you review the thesis.

lessons.title: Insurance
lessons.body:
Combined ratio = (claims + expenses) / net earned premium. Example: claims A$650m, expenses A$280m, premiums A$1,000m: 93%, an underwriting profit. Insurers also earn on investment float. Catastrophe events, reserve strengthening and reinsurance costs are key risks. Life insurers are sensitive to interest rates and longevity.

Why it matters: an insurer can look profitable until reserves prove thin or a catastrophe arrives.

Combined ratio = (claims + expenses) / net earned premium. Below 100% is an underwriting profit; above 100% is an underwriting loss. The fictional 93% (650 + 280) / 1,000 leaves investment income on float as additional, separate earnings. Life insurers add rate and longevity sensitivity.

Common error: treating last year's combined ratio as the expected cost of next year's catastrophe.

lessons.title: Market infrastructure and asset managers
lessons.body:
Exchanges and clearing houses earn per-trade, listing, data and clearing fees; revenues rise with volatility and volume. Payment networks earn per-transaction fees scaled with nominal spending. Asset managers earn fees on assets under management (AUM): revenue ~ AUM x fee rate, so market falls and outflows both hurt. Example: AUM A$100bn at 0.40% = A$400m revenue; a 15% market fall cuts it to A$340m before flows.

Why it matters: market-infrastructure and asset-management revenues often scale with activity or with asset prices.

Worked check: AUM A$100bn at 0.40% is A$400m of revenue. A 15% market fall with no flows leaves A$85bn and A$340m. Outflows make that worse. Exchange and payments volumes can rise in volatile years even as asset managers suffer.

These are GICS Financials business models alongside banks and insurers; do not analyse them as if they were loan books.

lessons.title: Deep dive: bank and insurer health check; practice case
lessons.body:
Fictional bank: loans A$600bn, deposits A$450bn, CET1 12.0%, NIM 1.90%, cost-to-income 47%, impairment charge 0.12% of loans. Stress test: if impairments rise to 0.60% of loans, the extra charge = 0.48% x 600bn = A$2.88bn pre-tax. If pre-provision profit is A$12bn, profit falls about 24% before tax effects. If capital stays above the regulator's requirements (APRA's in Australia; check current standards), the dividend may be maintained, but this is not certain. Insurer case: premium A$5bn, claims A$3.4bn, expenses A$1.4bn, combined ratio 96%. A catastrophe adding A$400m of net claims (after reinsurance) gives 104%, an underwriting loss; investment income on a A$9bn float at 4% (A$360m) partly offsets. Infrastructure case: an exchange with 60% of revenue from trading and clearing fees sees revenue rise in volatile years. An asset manager with A$80bn AUM at 0.45% earns A$360m; a 20% market fall plus 5% outflows gives 80 x 0.8 x 0.95 = A$60.8bn AUM and revenue of A$274m. Common errors: comparing CET1 across regulators without adjusting definitions; ignoring deposit concentration; treating insurer reserves as exact. Limitations: Basel standards are implemented differently by each national regulator (APRA in Australia).

Stress arithmetic check: extra impairments of 0.48% on A$600bn of loans equal A$2.88bn. Against A$12bn of pre-provision profit that is about 24% of that profit before tax. The lesson no longer claims capital is far above minima; it says that if capital remains above the relevant regulator's requirements the dividend may be maintained, but that is not certain. That wording should stay cautious.

Value cyclical sectors on mid-cycle assumptions

lessons.title: Energy value chain
lessons.body:
Upstream (exploration and production) earns price minus lifting cost and royalties; midstream (pipelines, storage) often earns fee-based tariffs; downstream (refining) earns crack spreads. Example: crude A$110/bbl, products A$135/bbl: crack ~ A$25/bbl. Metrics: production (boe/d), reserves (1P/2P), reserve life = reserves / annual production, breakeven price.

Energy (GICS Energy) metric interpretation. Upstream cash margin is roughly realised price minus lifting cost and royalties; reserve life = reserves / annual production; breakeven is the price at which a project or firm covers the cost definition the company is using (those definitions vary). Midstream fee-based tariffs are less directly tied to the commodity price. Downstream crack spread is refined-product value minus crude cost.

Worked reminder: reserve life 200m boe / 20m boe per year = 10 years. That is a ratio, not a promise the field produces evenly for a decade.

Spot-price valuation trap: multiplying last week's oil price by current production as if it were a perpetual annuity ignores decline, reinvestment and the cycle.

lessons.title: Mining
lessons.body:
Revenue ~ volume x price; cost metrics C1, AISC; grade (g/t gold, % copper) drives economics. Reserves vs resources differ in confidence. The JORC Code (2012) defines an Ore Reserve as the economically mineable part of a Measured and/or Indicated Mineral Resource, including dilution and loss allowances, defined by pre-feasibility or feasibility studies. Canada uses NI 43-101. Example: AISC A$2,300/oz, gold A$3,000/oz: margin A$700/oz; 400koz produced = A$280m all-in margin. Risks: sovereign, permitting, tailings, cost inflation.

Materials / mining metric interpretation. Grade (g/t or %) drives how much metal you get from a tonne of ore. AISC and C1 are cost metrics whose company definitions are not identical; read the reconciliation. JORC Ore Reserves are the economically mineable part of Measured and/or Indicated Mineral Resources, including dilution and losses, supported by pre-feasibility or feasibility studies (JORC Code 2012, as already cited). Resources are not automatically mineable. Other jurisdictions use other codes; this course does not treat SEC S-K 1300 as a verified parallel definition.

Worked reminder: gold A$3,200, AISC A$2,400, 250 koz gives (800 x 250,000) = A$200m of all-in margin before other corporate items.

lessons.title: Utilities
lessons.body:
Many networks are regulated: allowed revenue ~ regulated asset base (RAB) x allowed return + depreciation + opex. Example: RAB A$10bn, allowed return 6%: return component A$600m. Utilities are bond-like: higher rates often pressure valuations. Generators/retailers face wholesale price and fuel risk.

Utilities metric interpretation. Allowed return on a regulated asset base is a building block of allowed revenue, not a guaranteed shareholder return after gearing, opex overruns and regulatory resets. Example: RAB A$8bn times 5.5% = A$440m return component. Higher bond yields often pressure valuations because those cashflows are compared with bonds. Unregulated generation is a different, more commodity-like risk.

lessons.title: Transition risks
lessons.body:
Decarbonisation policy, carbon pricing, stranded asset risk and capex for renewables and grids shape long-run returns. Critical minerals (lithium, nickel, copper, rare earths) can boom and bust as supply responds. Treat ESG ratings critically; check methodology.

Transition and policy risks can change asset lives and required capex. Treat them as scenarios (carbon price, demand shift, permitting delay), not as a single ESG score. Critical-mineral prices can boom and bust as supply responds; that is cycle behaviour again.

lessons.title: Cycle behaviour
lessons.body:
Energy and mining are highly cyclical with operating leverage; shares often move before commodity prices. Use mid-cycle prices for valuation, not spot peaks.

Why mid-cycle thinking exists: energy and mining earnings swing with commodity prices and with operating leverage. Using spot peaks as the base for a multiple is how expensive assets look cheap. Write the commodity price you used in any valuation sentence.

Shares often move before the commodity as investors anticipate the next part of the cycle; that lead-lag is a tendency, not a timing system.

lessons.title: Deep dive: sector fundamentals for Energy, Materials and Utilities
lessons.body:
Energy (GICS Energy): key drivers are oil and gas prices, production growth, reserve replacement and capital discipline. Useful metrics: breakeven price, reserve life, net debt/EBITDA at mid-cycle prices, and production cost per boe. Case: a producer with 50m boe/yr production, cash cost A$30/boe and an oil price of A$90 earns A$3.0bn cash margin; at A$60 it earns A$1.5bn, so a 33% price fall halves the margin. Materials (miners, chemicals, construction materials): grade, recovery, AISC, strip ratio, mine life, sovereign risk, and Ore Reserves under JORC. Case: copper at A$13,000/t with C1 cost A$6,500/t on 200kt gives A$1.3bn; a 10% price fall cuts margin 20%. Utilities: a regulated asset base, allowed return, regulatory resets every few years, and gearing. Unregulated generators carry wholesale price risk. Common errors: valuing on spot prices; ignoring rehabilitation liabilities; assuming dividends are safe through regulatory resets. Limitations: resource estimates carry uncertainty; reserve definitions differ by reporting code (JORC in Australasia, and others elsewhere); compare definitions before comparing companies.

Cross-check of operating leverage: 50m boe at a A$60 cash margin (A$90 price minus A$30 cost) is A$3.0bn; at a A$30 margin (A$60 price) it is A$1.5bn. A one-third price fall halved the margin because costs are sticky. Use that pattern when you stress a producer, a miner, or (less directly) a commodity-linked utility input.

Analyse semiconductors and AI infrastructure cycles

Apply critical thinking to AI narratives
Identify platform, regulatory and geopolitical risks

lessons.title: Software metrics
lessons.body:
Annual recurring revenue (ARR), net revenue retention (NRR: revenue from last year's customers this year / last year), gross margin (often 70%+), and rule of 40 (revenue growth % + profit margin % >= 40). Example: growth 25%, FCF margin 12%: score 37. Stock-based compensation is a real cost; check dilution.

Information Technology / software metric interpretation. ARR is a company-defined run-rate of recurring revenue, not an IFRS line you can assume is comparable. NRR above 100% means existing customers spent more (up-sell net of churn); below 100% means the base shrank. Rule of 40 (growth % plus a profit-margin %) is a heuristic, not a law: 30% growth and 5% FCF margin scores 35. Stock-based compensation is a real economic cost because it dilutes owners.

Decision exercise: recompute FCF after subtracting SBC and see whether the quality story changes, as in the later deep-dive case.

lessons.title: Semiconductors and AI infrastructure
lessons.body:
Chips are cyclical: inventory builds and cuts cause swings. Segments: design, foundry, equipment, memory. AI demand drives data-centre capex (GPUs, networking, power, cooling). Metrics: book-to-bill, inventory days, capex guidance of large cloud providers. Concentration: a few customers may dominate revenue.

Semiconductors and AI-infrastructure metric interpretation. Book-to-bill below 1 means new orders are running behind current billings, often an early-cycle warning. Inventory days rising while book-to-bill falls is a classic correction signal, not a proof of disaster. Customer concentration (a few cloud buyers of AI chips, for example) is a risk metric as much as a growth story.

Capex guidance from large purchasers can move an entire supplier set. Treat it as demand colour, and remember guidance changes.

lessons.title: Communications
lessons.body:
Telecoms: ARPU, churn, subscribers, capex/revenue (often high for networks), spectrum costs, leverage. Media and platforms: users (DAU/MAU), engagement, ad revenue per user, content costs. Example: 10m subscribers at A$50 ARPU/month = A$6bn annual revenue; 1% monthly churn means ~11.4% of the base lost per year (1-0.99^12).

Communication Services metric interpretation. Telecoms: ARPU, churn, subscribers, capex/revenue and leverage. High capex intensity is normal for networks; FCF after spectrum outlays can look very different from EBITDA. Platforms: users, engagement and ad revenue per user. User growth without monetisation is not revenue.

Worked reminder: 10 million subscribers at A$50 a month is A$6bn a year. Monthly churn of 2% compounds to about 1 - 0.98^12 = 21.5% of the starting base over a year if there are no adds (the lesson's similar example used 1%).

lessons.title: AI narratives critically
lessons.body:
Separate revenue already earned from AI from plans and hopes. Ask: who pays, at what margin, with what competition, and what capex is required? Hype cycles have repeatedly overshot (e.g. the dot-com era). Also apply this to AI trading tools: they make errors and can be confidently wrong.

Why it matters: narrative-heavy sectors reward people who separate booked revenue from plans.

Ask who pays today, at what margin, with what capex and with what competition. Apply the same scepticism to AI trading tools: fluency is not verification. A claim without a primary source stays in the unverified column.

lessons.title: Platform and regulatory risks
lessons.body:
Antitrust, privacy rules, content regulation, export controls on chips, and cybersecurity incidents can change economics quickly. Network effects can protect incumbents but also invite regulation.

Platform and regulatory risks (antitrust, privacy, content rules, export controls, cyber incidents) can change a multiple faster than a quarterly KPI. Write them as scenario risks with a size implication (reduce, hedge, or avoid) rather than as footnotes you ignore until they hit the headline.

lessons.title: Deep dive: Information Technology and Communication Services fundamentals
lessons.body:
Information Technology (software, hardware, semiconductors, IT services). Software: ARR growth, NRR, gross margin, rule of 40, stock-based compensation as a % of revenue, and FCF after SBC. Case: revenue A$1bn, FCF A$250m, SBC A$180m. FCF after SBC is A$70m, a 7% margin, not 25%. Semiconductors: book-to-bill, inventory days, customer concentration and capex cycles. Case: inventory days rising from 90 to 150 while book-to-bill falls to 0.8 signals a likely correction. Communication Services (telecom, media, interactive platforms): ARPU, churn, subscriber net adds, capex intensity, spectrum costs; for platforms, users, engagement and ad revenue per user. Case: a telecom with ARPU A$55 and 8m subscribers earns A$5.28bn a year; capex at 18% of revenue (A$950m) plus spectrum renewals limits FCF. AI claims checklist: revenue already recognised versus pipeline; incremental margin; capex and power needs; customer concentration; regulatory exposure. Common errors: extrapolating peak growth; ignoring dilution; confusing user growth with monetisation. Limitations: company-defined metrics such as ARR and DAU are non-standard; compare definitions.

SBC adjustment check: FCF A$250m minus SBC A$180m leaves A$70m, a 7% margin rather than 25%, on A$1bn of revenue. If you use the unadjusted figure to claim quality, you are choosing a definition that hides dilution. State the choice.

objectives.text: Analyse industrials via backlog, margins and cyclicality
Analyse consumer staples and discretionary via volume/price and same-store sales
Analyse health care via pipelines, patents and reimbursement
Analyse REITs via NTA, FFO, gearing and WALE
Use GICS sector classification and rotation tendencies

lessons.title: Industrials
lessons.body:
Includes capital goods, transport, airlines, defence, construction. Metrics: order backlog, book-to-bill, EBIT margin, working capital. Airlines: load factor, RASK minus CASK. Example: RASK 12.0c, CASK 11.2c: unit margin 0.8c per available seat-km; a 5% fuel cost rise can wipe this out.

Industrials metric interpretation. Backlog coverage = backlog / annual revenue; book-to-bill above 1 usually means the backlog is growing. Fixed-price contracts transfer cost-overrun risk to the contractor: a 5% overrun on a A$1bn job is A$50m. Airlines: load factor, RASK (revenue per available seat-km) minus CASK (cost per available seat-km). A 0.4c negative gap means the airline loses that amount on every available seat-km before other items; fuel and FX can erase a thin positive gap.

lessons.title: Consumer staples vs discretionary
lessons.body:
Staples (food, household products, supermarkets) are defensive; analyse volume vs price/mix and gross margin. Discretionary (retail, autos, travel, restaurants) is cyclical; analyse same-store (like-for-like) sales, inventory turnover, and consumer confidence. Example: revenue +6% = price +8%, volume -2%: growth driven by price, which may not last.

Consumer Staples versus Consumer Discretionary metric interpretation. Staples: split growth into volume versus price/mix and watch gross margin; price-led growth can fade when consumers trade down to private label. Discretionary: same-store (like-for-like) sales = traffic x ticket; inventory turns; and sensitivity to consumer credit and confidence. One quarter is not a trend.

Worked reminder: revenue +6% = price +8% and volume -2% is price-led. Ask whether volume can keep falling without becoming a volume problem.

lessons.title: Health care
lessons.body:
Pharma/biotech: pipelines by phase (Phase I-III success rates are low), patent cliffs, regulator approvals: the TGA regulates therapeutic goods in Australia (goods generally must be on the ARTG before supply, and it does not consider cost-effectiveness or subsidy, which sits with the PBS and other areas of government); the US FDA is responsible for ensuring the safety, efficacy and security of drugs, biologics and devices; EMA's scientific committees give recommendations that form the basis for EU centralised authorisation. Devices and services: procedure volumes, reimbursement rates. Insurers/hospitals: utilisation. Binary events (trial results) can move share prices 50%+ either way; size accordingly.

Health Care metric interpretation. Pipelines should be listed by phase without inventing success-rate percentages this course has not sourced. Patent cliffs are scheduled revenue risks. Reimbursement (who pays, at what rate) can matter as much as science. Regulator roles taught here: TGA (Australia; ARTG listing; not the subsidy decision), FDA (US safety, efficacy and security of drugs, biologics and devices), and EMA scientific recommendations as a basis for EU centralised authorisation. Binary trial results can move prices violently; size as event risk, not as ordinary swing risk.

lessons.title: Real estate and REITs
lessons.body:
REITs own property and distribute most income. Metrics: net tangible assets (NTA) per security, funds from operations (FFO), gearing = net debt / total assets, occupancy, weighted average lease expiry (WALE), cap rate = net operating income / property value. Example: NOI A$50m, value A$1bn: cap rate 5%. If cap rates rise to 5.5%, value = 50/0.055 = A$909m (-9.1%).

Real Estate / REIT metric interpretation. Cap rate = NOI / value, so value = NOI / cap rate. If NOI is A$30m and the cap rate is 6%, value is A$500m. If cap rates rise from 5% to 6% on A$60m of NOI, value falls from A$1.2bn to A$1.0bn, about -16.7%. Gearing = net debt / total assets (common disclosure; check the REIT's definition). WALE is the weighted average lease expiry; a short WALE with falling occupancy is a different risk than a long WALE to strong tenants. Valuations can lag traded markets, so NTA is not a hard floor.

lessons.title: Sector rotation
lessons.body:
Defensives (staples, utilities, health) often outperform in slowdowns; cyclicals (industrials, discretionary, materials) in recoveries. This is a tendency, not a rule; GICS (MSCI and S&P Dow Jones Indices) has 11 sectors, 25 industry groups, 74 industries and 163 sub-industries per the MSCI methodology dated Aug 2024: Energy, Materials, Industrials, Consumer Discretionary, Consumer Staples, Health Care, Financials, Information Technology, Communication Services, Utilities, Real Estate.

GICS coverage check. MSCI and S&P Dow Jones Indices describe GICS as 11 sectors, 25 industry groups, 74 industries and 163 sub-industries (methodology dated August 2024, evidence E17): Energy, Materials, Industrials, Consumer Discretionary, Consumer Staples, Health Care, Financials, Information Technology, Communication Services, Utilities and Real Estate. Sector-rotation stories (defensives in slowdowns, cyclicals in recoveries) are tendencies, not rules, and they do not replace unit-metric work.

If you cannot name a useful metric for each of those 11 sectors, return to Modules 12 to 15 before treating a rotation call as analysis.

lessons.title: Deep dive: Industrials, Consumer Discretionary, Consumer Staples, Health Care and Real Estate fundamentals
lessons.body:
Industrials: backlog coverage (backlog/annual revenue), book-to-bill, margin on fixed-price contracts, working capital; airlines: load factor and RASK-CASK, fuel hedging. Case: a contractor with A$6bn backlog against A$3bn revenue has 2 years of coverage, but fixed-price risk means a 5% cost overrun on a A$1bn job erases A$50m. Consumer Discretionary: same-store sales split into traffic x ticket, gross margin, inventory turns, and consumer credit. Case: same-store sales +3% = ticket +6%, traffic -3%; customers are buying less often. Consumer Staples: volume versus price/mix, private-label competition, input costs. Health Care: pipeline by phase, patent expiry schedule, reimbursement, and regulator approvals (TGA in Australia, FDA in the US, EMA in the EU). Case: a drug that is 40% of revenue loses patent protection in 2 years; plan for generic erosion. Real Estate: cap rate, NTA, gearing, WALE, occupancy, interest cover; the office, industrial, retail and residential sub-sectors differ. Case: a REIT with gearing at 38% and a covenant at 50%. If valuations fall 15%, assets fall from A$10bn to A$8.5bn with debt of A$3.8bn: gearing 44.7%, near the limit. Common errors: treating all REITs alike; ignoring lease incentives; reading one quarter of same-store sales as a trend.

Integrated decision exercise: take one name from each remaining GICS sector you have not already used this week and write, in one line each, the metric, the number, the definition, and one limitation (company-defined metric, cyclical base, regulatory reset, binary event, or valuation lag). That list is the practical evidence for this module, not a profit target.

objectives.text: Read key macro releases
Explain surprise vs expectations pricing
Map company and index catalysts
Assess news quality using primary sources
Run a calendar-driven event-risk process

lessons.title: Macro releases
lessons.body:
Inflation (CPI, trimmed mean, core PCE), labour (unemployment, payrolls, wages), activity (GDP, retail sales, PMIs; S&P Global describes its PMI diffusion indexes as ranging 0-100, where 50.0 means no change on the previous month, above 50.0 an improvement and below 50.0 a deterioration. Other providers such as ISM publish their own PMIs; check their methodology), and trade data. National statistics agencies (e.g. ABS, US BLS, Eurostat, ONS) publish schedules in advance. Central bank meetings and minutes drive rate expectations. Example source: the ABS publishes Australia's Consumer Price Index and trimmed-mean inflation in its 'Consumer Price Index, Australia' releases.

Why it matters: traders do not trade the printed number in isolation; they trade how it compares with what was already priced. Knowing who publishes a series, what it measures, and when it is released (including the publisher's time zone) is part of reading it.

Decision exercise (fictional paper): two inflation prints land the same week. Series A is a headline CPI figure from a national statistics agency. Series B is a trimmed-mean or core measure from the same agency. Write which one your paper rate-sensitive position should treat as more relevant and why, then check the agency's own description rather than a social-media summary.

Limitations and common errors: series are revised; seasonal adjustment methods change; and one month is not a trend. Do not treat a PMI from one provider as if every PMI used the same construction. S&P Global's 50.0 no-change wording applies to its PMIs; other providers publish their own methodologies. Timestamps without a time zone invite look-ahead mistakes when you combine US, European and Australian releases.

lessons.title: Surprise matters
lessons.body:
Markets price expectations. Example: consensus CPI 3.0%, actual 3.4% = +0.4pp surprise; bond yields may jump even though inflation 'only' rose slightly. A strong result already expected can lead to a fall ('buy the rumour, sell the fact'). Compare to consensus and to what is priced (e.g. rate futures implied probabilities).

Why it matters: a strong print that matches consensus can be a non-event, while a small miss can reprice an entire rate path.

Worked decision (fictional): consensus unemployment is 4.1% and the print is 4.1%, but wage growth prints 0.4 percentage points above consensus. Bond yields rise. The labour-market headline was not the surprise; the wage component was. Journal the surprise, not only the level.

Common errors: confusing a forecast beat with a profitable trade; ignoring what rate futures already implied; and treating after-the-fact narratives as if they were your pre-trade thesis. If you cannot state the consensus and the implied move before the release, you are not prepared to trade the event.

lessons.title: Company catalysts
lessons.body:
Earnings and guidance changes, dividends, buybacks, M&A, capital raisings, index inclusion/exclusion, regulatory decisions, trial results, and lock-up expiries. ASX Listing Rule 3.1 (quoted in Guidance Note 8, May 2024) says that once an entity becomes aware of information a reasonable person would expect to have a material effect on the price or value of its securities, it must immediately tell ASX, subject to the Rule 3.1A exceptions. Moneysmart (ASIC) explains that in Australia insider trading includes trading while knowing non-public information that could affect price, and that recommending, suggesting or tipping others is also illegal. ASIC RG 264 summarises 'inside information' (s1042A Corporations Act) as information that is not generally available and that a reasonable person would expect to have a material effect on price or value. Other jurisdictions have their own laws; this is general education, not legal advice.

Why it matters: company-level catalysts can dwarf a well-reasoned valuation view in a single session. Sizing before a binary event is a risk decision, not an afterthought.

Decision exercise: pick one listed company and build a one-week catalyst calendar from primary sources only (exchange announcements, official regulator or court lists, published earnings dates). Mark any item you found only on social media as unverified. Decide in advance whether your paper position will be cut, held, or avoided.

Limitations: continuous-disclosure rules and insider-trading laws differ by jurisdiction. The ASX and ASIC wording in this module is general education about Australia, not legal advice and not a statement of penalties. When in doubt, do not trade on information that may not be public.

lessons.title: News quality
lessons.body:
Distinguish primary sources (company announcements, central bank statements, official statistics) from commentary and social media. Check timestamps, avoid trading headlines you cannot verify, beware AI-generated or fake news. Ask: is this new, material, and not already priced?

Why it matters: bad information is an execution and ethics risk, not just an inconvenience.

A practical verification sequence: (1) identify the original publisher; (2) open that publisher's page or filing, not a screenshot; (3) note the time zone and whether the item is new; (4) ask what would falsify it; (5) if you cannot complete those steps, the default is no new paper trade.

Common errors: forwarding an AI summary that invented a source; treating a blog recap as a filing; and ignoring that some news is recycled commentary on an announcement from days earlier.

lessons.title: Event risk process
lessons.body:
Keep a weekly calendar; reduce size or avoid opening new positions just before binary events unless the event is the planned thesis; pre-define what result invalidates the trade. Example rule: halve paper position size if a scheduled event's implied move exceeds 2x normal daily range.

Why it matters: event risk is where otherwise careful sizing gets abandoned just this once.

Decision exercise: write a one-line rule that states when you will not open a new paper position (for example, implied event move more than twice the recent daily range, or an unverified headline). Then apply it to next week's calendar. Strategic no-trading is a valid output of a risk process.

Common errors: adding size into an event to make back an earlier loss; holding a leveraged product into a binary print against plan; and changing the rule after you see the number.

lessons.title: Deep dive: event-risk playbook and news verification case
lessons.body:
Weekly routine: (1) list scheduled events (central bank decisions, CPI, jobs, earnings, index rebalances); (2) note consensus and implied moves where free data exist; (3) mark positions exposed to each event; (4) apply pre-set sizing rules; (5) after each event, log surprise, reaction and whether your plan held. Case (fictional): CPI consensus 0.6% q/q, actual 0.9%. Two-year yields jump 15 bps, and your paper long in a rate-sensitive REIT drops 4% at the open. Your rule said to halve REIT exposure before CPI; you did not. The journal entry records a rule breach, the cost and a remediation. News case: a social post claims a miner has 'lost its licence'. Check the company's exchange announcements and the regulator; ASX Listing Rule 3.1 requires immediate disclosure of market-sensitive information, so absence of an announcement is itself informative but not conclusive (trading halts may be pending). Common errors: trading the headline rather than the surprise; ignoring time zones (US releases land overnight for Australia); trusting screenshots; confusing correlation with causation after the fact.

Timezone and session addendum: a US CPI release at 08:30 Eastern Time is already afternoon or evening in Australia. If your data stamp is stored as a naive local time, a backtest can accidentally treat that print as known during the Australian cash session. Always store event times with an explicit time zone and convert before deciding whether information was available.

The playbook's purpose is process evidence: you can show you listed the event, sized in advance, and journaled any breach. It is not a claim that following a calendar makes event trading profitable.

modules.title: Technical Analysis: Trend, Mean Reversion and Volatility

objectives.text: Use moving averages and breakouts to define trend
Use z-scores and oscillators for mean reversion
Measure volatility with ATR and standard deviation
Test technical rules honestly rather than trusting chart patterns

lessons.title: Trend tools
lessons.body:
Simple moving average (SMA) = average of last N closes. A common trend filter: price above 200-day SMA. Breakout: price exceeds N-day high. Trend rules tend to have low win rates but larger winners; they suffer in choppy markets.

Why it matters: a moving average is only a description of past prices. It becomes a trading rule only when you specify entry, exit, size and costs.

Decision exercise: write close greater than the 200-day simple moving average as a complete rule, including whether you trade the close or the next open. If you cannot state the fill, you do not yet have a testable idea.

Limitations: the 200-day choice is a convention, not a law. In strong trends it can keep you in; in ranges it can whipsaw. Never treat a single moving-average cross as proof of an edge.

lessons.title: Mean reversion
lessons.body:
Z-score = (price - mean)/standard deviation over a lookback. Example: 20-day mean A$50, sd A$2, price A$46: z = -2.0. RSI measures recent gains vs losses (0-100; <30 'oversold'). Mean reversion tends to work better in range-bound markets and fails when a new trend begins.

Why it matters: mean-reversion tools describe how extended a price is versus a recent window. They do not know whether the window is still the relevant regime.

Worked check: z = (46 - 50) / 2 = -2.0 says the price is two standard deviations below a 20-day mean. That can be a fading candidate in a range or the first day of a decline. The tool cannot tell you which.

Common errors: buying every oversold print; changing the lookback after a loss so that the last signal would have been skipped; and forgetting that a z-score uses the same prices that already moved against you.

lessons.title: Volatility
lessons.body:
Average true range (ATR) = average of max(high-low, |high-prev close|, |low-prev close|). Annualised volatility ~ daily sd x sqrt(N), where N is the number of trading periods per year. 252 is a common convention for exchange-traded assets; 365 is often used for 24/7 crypto. The square-root rule assumes independent returns, so state your assumption. Example: daily sd 1.2%: about 19% annual. Volatility clusters: calm and turbulent periods persist. Implied volatility (from options, e.g. VIX for S&P 500) reflects expected volatility.

Why annualisation needs a stated convention: multiplying a daily standard deviation by the square root of 252 is a common method for exchange-traded assets that rest on weekends. Using 365 is a common choice for assets that price every calendar day, such as many crypto markets. Both assume returns are independent enough that variance adds linearly with time. If returns are serially correlated, that square-root rule misstates horizon risk. Always write the factor you used (252, 365, 12 for monthly, or another) and do not mix frequencies inside one statistic.

Decision exercise: a daily standard deviation of 1.0% annualises to about 15.9% with sqrt(252) and about 19.1% with sqrt(365). The gap is a convention choice, not extra skill.

lessons.title: Support, resistance and patterns
lessons.body:
Support and resistance are zones where buying/selling previously appeared. Patterns (head-and-shoulders, flags) are subjective; different people draw different lines. Convert any idea into an exact rule before testing.

Why it matters: two people can look at the same chart and draw different support lines. That subjectivity is why patterns must be turned into rules before they can be tested.

Decision exercise: pick one pattern you like and write entry, invalidation and exit without pointing at a picture. If you need the picture to define the rule, it is not yet testable.

Common errors: drawing the line after the bounce; ignoring that many others see the same round number; and treating a pattern name as evidence.

lessons.title: Testing rules
lessons.body:
Write the rule exactly (entry, exit, sizing, costs). Test across markets and periods, include costs, count trades, and compare to buy-and-hold. Without testing, chart reading is storytelling. Module 20 covers bias.

Why it matters: an untested chart story cannot be distinguished from hindsight.

Minimum test package before you trust a paper rule: exact definition, more than one market or period, costs and delays, trade count, and a comparison with a naive benchmark such as buy-and-hold or random entries with the same exits. Module 20 then asks whether the test itself was honest.

lessons.title: Deep dive: turning a chart idea into a testable rule
lessons.body:
Idea: 'buy pullbacks in uptrends'. Exact rule: universe of 50 liquid large caps; trend filter close > 200-day SMA; entry when the 3-day RSI is below 15 at the close, buying the next open; exit when close > 5-day SMA or after 10 days; stop at 2 x 14-day ATR; risk 0.5% per trade; costs of 10 bps per side plus 5 bps slippage. Every term is now measurable, and the rule can be tested and falsified. Worked ATR stop: ATR A$1.20, entry A$48.00, stop A$45.60, risk per share A$2.40. With A$500 of risk the size is 208 shares. Volatility scaling: if realised vol doubles, ATR roughly doubles and size halves. Common errors: drawing trendlines after the fact; changing parameters after losses; optimising lookbacks to the decimal; ignoring that 'oversold' can stay oversold; testing only in one bull market. Limitations: indicator settings are conventions, not laws; most simple technical rules show weak or unstable edges after costs, so test before trusting.

Link to data quality: the exact rule above still fails if the price series is wrong. A split-unadjusted series can create a false breakdown. A timezone-naive series can create a false close-already-known-at-the-open signal. Test the rule on a series you can explain, including how corporate actions and missing bars were handled. The school's synthetic mini-backtest (datasets/synthetic_mini_backtest.csv) is a practice file for those checks, not a source of market edge.

modules.title: Position Sizing, Correlation, Stops and Gaps

objectives.text: Size positions by fixed fractional risk
Adapt size to volatility (ATR)
Use correlation to understand concentration
Design stops with realistic gap risk
Apply drawdown limits, heat caps and kill switches

lessons.title: Fixed fractional sizing
lessons.body:
Risk per trade = account x risk %. Shares = risk / (entry - stop). Example (fictional): A$100,000 paper account, 0.5% risk = A$500; entry A$25.00, stop A$23.75 (A$1.25): 400 shares = A$10,000 position. Many professionals keep per-trade risk to a small fraction of capital.

Why it matters: most large trading failures begin with a position that was too large for the stop distance, not with a wrong opinion about direction.

The formula shares = (account x risk %) / (entry - stop) assumes you actually will exit near that stop. If the market can gap, the realised loss can exceed the planned R. Size is therefore a plan, not a guarantee.

Decision exercise (fictional): account A$80,000, risk 0.75%, entry A$12.40, stop A$11.80. Planned risk = A$600. Stop distance = A$0.60. Size = 1,000 shares, notional A$12,400. Write whether a 3x gap through the stop would still be acceptable under your heat rule. If not, cut size or skip the trade.

Common errors: using account percentage of notional instead of account percentage of risk; placing the stop after you see the fill; and rounding size up to make it worth it.

lessons.title: Volatility sizing
lessons.body:
Set stop distance in ATR multiples (e.g. 2 x ATR) so size adapts: if ATR A$0.80, stop distance A$1.60; at A$500 risk, 312 shares. Higher volatility, smaller size.

Why it matters: a fixed share count in a quiet week becomes an oversized bet when volatility doubles.

Worked case: risk A$400, ATR A$1.00, stop at 2 x ATR = A$2.00, size = 200 shares. If ATR rises to A$2.00, the same rule produces 100 shares. That is the point of volatility sizing: it translates a money risk cap into fewer shares when the market is moving more.

Limitation: ATR is backward-looking. It will not warn you the day before a gap. Treat it as an adapter, not a forecast.

lessons.title: Correlation
lessons.body:
Correlation (-1 to +1) measures co-movement. Five 'different' bank shares with 0.8 correlation behave like one large position. Portfolio variance for two assets: w1^2 s1^2 + w2^2 s2^2 + 2 w1 w2 rho s1 s2. Example: 50/50, each 20% vol, rho 0.5: variance = 0.01+0.01+0.01 = 0.03; vol 17.3%. With rho 1.0: 20%. Correlations tend to rise in crises.

Why it matters: correlation is how diversification succeeds or fails. It is not stable.

Correlation-regime case (fictional numbers, for process practice, not a historical index claim): in a calm window four bank shares show pairwise correlations around 0.55. You treat four 0.50% risk slots as separate and record 2.0% heat. In a stress week the same pairs print realized correlations around 0.90. The four slots now behave much more like one concentrated 2% bet. The heat number did not change; the independence assumption did.

Decision exercise: group your current paper positions by a shared driver (same sector, same commodity, same currency, same rates view). Cap each group, not only the sum of stops. When you cannot estimate correlation honestly, assume it is high.

Limitations: a single correlation number is an average of a window. It can be low right up until the window that hurts you. No correlation estimate guarantees that diversification will work in the next crisis.

lessons.title: Stops and gaps
lessons.body:
Stops limit typical losses but gaps skip them. Example: 400 shares, stop A$23.75, gap open A$21.00: loss = 400 x 4.00 = A$1,600, 3.2x planned risk. Stress test: assume worst plausible gap (e.g. 3x normal) for overnight and event positions. Options or smaller size can cap gap risk.

Why it matters: a stop is an instruction about ordinary paths. Gaps, halted trading and thin books can send the fill far beyond the instruction.

Gap and liquidity stress (fictional): 500 shares, entry A$20.00, stop A$19.20, planned risk A$400. An overnight announcement opens the share at A$17.60 on a wide A$17.40/A$17.90 quote with little depth. A stop-market order can fill near A$17.60 or worse if it walks a thin book: realised loss about A$1,200, or 3R, before brokerage. If you needed that exit during a trading halt, you may not be able to trade at all until the auction, which can be further away.

Decision exercise: before any overnight or event-held paper position, write a gap multiple you are willing to accept (for example 3x the planned stop distance) and the resulting stressed loss. If that stressed loss breaches your per-trade or group cap, reduce size or do not hold through the event.

Common errors: believing a stop caps the loss at exactly 1R; using marketable orders that are large relative to displayed depth; and treating paper fills at the stop price as realistic for live gaps. Nothing in this module guarantees a maximum drawdown.

lessons.title: Drawdown limits
lessons.body:
Pre-set rules: e.g. cut size by half after a 5% account drawdown; pause new trades after 10% and review. Firm-level heat cap: total open risk (sum of stop distances) e.g. <= 3% of equity. Rules must be written before trading.

Why it matters: drawdown ladders and heat caps are pre-commitments you make while calm so that you do not negotiate with yourself while losing.

They are not forecasts and they are not guarantees. A 10% pause rule does not mean the account cannot fall more than 10%: correlated gaps, skipped stops and added risk can all drive a deeper path. State that clearly in any paper risk policy.

Value at risk and expected shortfall (definitions). The Basel Committee's market-risk terminology (Minimum capital requirements for market risk, January 2019 rev. February 2019, MAR10.17-10.18) describes value at risk (VaR) as a measure of the worst expected loss on a portfolio of instruments resulting from market movements over a given time horizon and a pre-defined confidence level, and expected shortfall (ES) as a measure of the average of all potential losses exceeding the VaR at that confidence level. Those are regulatory-terminology definitions for bank market risk, used here as clear public wording. They are not a claim that a retail paper account must run a bank internal model, and they are not a maximum-loss promise.

Worked historical-style illustration (fictional sample, not market data): suppose 100 equally likely daily P&L outcomes, and the five worst losses are 2.4%, 1.9%, 1.6%, 1.4% and 1.3% of equity. A common teaching reading of one-day 95% historical VaR is the fifth-percentile loss, 1.3% of equity (A$1,300 on A$100,000). An inclusive average of those five tail losses, a teaching stand-in for expected shortfall at the same cutoff, is (2.4 + 1.9 + 1.6 + 1.4 + 1.3) / 5 = 1.72% (A$1,720). Basel's wording says ES averages losses exceeding VaR; some implementations average the tail at or beyond the cutoff. State which sample rule you used. Either way, ES is larger than VaR because it describes how bad the tail is, not only where the tail begins.

Limitations you must be able to recite: VaR does not say how large losses beyond the cutoff can be; a 95% VaR of A$1,300 does not cap the loss at A$1,300. Historical VaR assumes the sample window represents the future and can miss a new crisis. That is a stationarity assumption: the method treats the sample as if future returns come from the same distribution (and, for many parametric versions, as if returns are independent over the horizon). Markets are non-stationary and returns cluster, so a calm window can understate the next shock. Parametric VaR that assumes a thin-tailed distribution can understate crash risk. Neither VaR nor ES is a drawdown figure: drawdown is a multi-day path. Neither includes the extra loss from exiting a larger size than the market can absorb (liquidity horizon, MAR10.20, is the time assumed to be required to exit or hedge without materially affecting prices in stressed conditions). A calm-window VaR that used low correlations will be too small if correlations rise. No risk statistic, stop, or ladder guarantees the next drawdown.

lessons.title: Deep dive: portfolio heat and correlated-risk worked case
lessons.body:
Fictional paper account, A$100,000, rule of 0.5% per trade and a 3% heat cap. Open positions: four Australian banks, each with A$500 risk to stop; two iron-ore miners at A$500 each; one US tech at A$500. Gross heat = 7 x 500 = A$3,500 = 3.5%, over the cap. Correlation grouping: the four banks (pairwise correlation about 0.8) behave closer to one A$2,000 bet. A rule might cap any correlated group at 1.5% (A$1,500), so trim the banks to three or reduce size. Gap stress: assume a 3x overnight gap through stops for the miners; their risk becomes A$3,000, so the stressed total = 2,000 + 3,000 + 500 = A$5,500 (5.5%). Drawdown ladder (proposed default): at -5% from peak, halve new risk to 0.25%; at -10%, stop new entries and complete a mistake review; resume only after a written review. Common errors: counting positions instead of risk; moving stops further away; adding to losers; ignoring correlation spikes in crises. Limitations: correlations are unstable; stress multiples are assumptions, not forecasts.

Crisis and correlation addendum (process case, fictional): imagine your paper book holds three iron-ore producers and two Australian banks into a risk-off week. Individual stops still sum to 2.5% heat, under a 3% cap. On the stress Monday all five gap down together as the shared drivers (China demand news and a jump in funding costs) move at once. Pairwise realized correlations jump, liquidity thins, and two of the stops fill beyond the planned price. Stressed loss is larger than both headline heat and any calm-window VaR you had scribbled from the previous month.

What the case is for: practising group caps, gap multiples, and the decision to trade or not trade. What it is not: a prediction of any named historical crash, a template that the next crisis will match, or a promise that following the ladder would have kept the loss inside a published number.

If a calculation or an uploaded AI recommendation says you may exceed the heat cap because VaR looks fine, decline it. Risk limits outrank a single statistic.

modules.title: Performance Metrics and Statistical Confidence

objectives.text: Calculate win rate, payoff ratio, expectancy and R-multiples
Calculate Sharpe and Sortino ratios
Judge sample size and confidence
Report metrics honestly

lessons.title: R-multiples and expectancy
lessons.body:
R = initial risk per trade. A trade risking A$500 that makes A$1,000 is +2R. Expectancy per trade = win rate x average win - loss rate x average loss. Example: 40% wins averaging 2.5R, 60% losses averaging 1R: E = 0.4x2.5 - 0.6x1 = +0.40R. Payoff ratio = avg win / avg loss = 2.5.

Why it matters: R converts every trade into the same risk units so that a A$200 win on a A$100 risk and a A$2,000 win on a A$1,000 risk are both +2R. Without that, you cannot compare process quality across different sizes.

Decision exercise: from your last five paper trades, compute each R-multiple using the planned stop distance, not the realised gap, if you want the process view, and also record the realised multiple if a gap occurred. Expectancy uses whatever definition you pre-commit to; changing it after the fact is a reporting error.

Limitation: expectancy is an average. A positive average with a few huge winners can hide a strategy that usually loses.

lessons.title: Win rate is not enough
lessons.body:
A 90% win-rate strategy with average win 0.1R and average loss 1.5R: E = 0.09 - 0.15 = -0.06R, a loser. Profit factor = gross profit / gross loss.

Why it matters: marketing for trading services often leads with win rate because it sounds like skill. The arithmetic does not care.

Worked reminder: 80% winners of 0.2R and 20% losers of 1.2R gives 0.16 - 0.24 = -0.08R. High accuracy, negative expectancy. Always pair win rate with payoff and with costs.

lessons.title: Sharpe and Sortino
lessons.body:
Sharpe = (return - risk-free) / standard deviation of returns. Example: 12% return, 4% risk-free, 16% vol: Sharpe 0.5. Sortino uses downside deviation: with downside deviation 10%, Sortino = 0.8. Annualise consistently; serial correlation and fat tails distort Sharpe. Origin: William F. Sharpe introduced the measure in 1966 as the 'reward-to-variability ratio'. His 1994 article 'The Sharpe Ratio' defines it on excess return over a benchmark and warns that annualising assumes no serial correlation; specific samples can violate this. In practice, state the risk-free or benchmark rate used, the return frequency and the annualisation factor.

Sharpe annualisation, stated carefully. If you compute a Sharpe ratio from daily excess returns with mean mu_d and standard deviation sigma_d, a common annualisation is (mu_d / sigma_d) times sqrt(N), where N is 252 for many exchange-traded series or another stated factor. Equivalently, annualise the mean by multiplying by N and the standard deviation by sqrt(N), then divide. Sharpe's 1994 article warns that such annualising assumes no serial correlation; if returns are autocorrelated, the annualised figure is distorted. Do not annualise a two-week sample and present it as a comparable yearly Sharpe. State the risk-free or benchmark series, the return frequency, and N.

Sortino replaces total volatility with downside deviation, so two strategies with the same Sharpe can have different Sortino ratios if one has more upside volatility. Neither ratio is a promise of future returns, and both can look attractive on short, lucky samples.

Decision exercise: using fictional monthly excess returns with mean 0.8% and standard deviation 2.0%, a monthly Sharpe is 0.40. Multiplying by sqrt(12) gives about 1.39 only if you accept the independence assumption. Write that assumption next to the number.

lessons.title: Sample size and confidence
lessons.body:
Standard error of mean R = sd(R)/sqrt(n). Example: mean 0.3R, sd 1.5R, n = 25: SE = 0.3; t = 1.0, weak evidence. n = 225: SE = 0.1, t = 3.0, stronger. Rough rule: fewer than ~30 trades says little; even hundreds can mislead if regimes change.

Why it matters: without a standard error you cannot tell a real-looking average from noise.

A confidence interval that includes zero means you have not established a positive edge, even if the point estimate is positive. That is a reason for patience or for more data, not a reason to increase size. Regime change can make even a large historical sample misleading.

lessons.title: Honest reporting
lessons.body:
Report: number of trades, period, net of costs, max drawdown, best/worst trades, exposure time, and paper vs live. Never report only winners, cherry-picked windows or gross returns. Past performance does not guarantee future results.

Why it matters: the easiest way to invent skill is to hide trades, costs, or losing periods.

An honest paper statement labels itself paper, states the content version of any rules, and separates human-discretion results from AI-assisted or uploaded-strategy results. Mixing those tracks is a reporting error.

lessons.title: Deep dive: reading a performance report critically
lessons.body:
Fictional 120-trade paper report: win rate 42%, average win 1.9R, average loss 1.0R. Expectancy = 0.42 x 1.9 - 0.58 x 1.0 = 0.798 - 0.580 = +0.218R. Standard deviation of R is 1.6. SE = 1.6/sqrt(120) = 0.146, t = 1.49, so the evidence is weak. A 95% interval is roughly 0.218 +/- 1.98 x 0.146 = -0.07R to +0.51R, which includes zero. Profit factor = (0.42 x 1.9)/(0.58 x 1.0) = 1.38. Max drawdown 11R; the longest losing streak was 9. Probability check: with a 58% loss rate, a 9-loss streak somewhere in 120 trades is not unusual (a simple simulation of independent trades gives about a 30% chance). Process versus luck: the top 3 trades contributed 40% of profit; removing them gives expectancy of about +0.10R, so the result is fragile. Common errors: quoting win rate alone; annualising Sharpe from overlapping or daily-autocorrelated returns without adjustment; comparing strategies over different periods; ignoring the dependence of results on a few outliers. Limitations: normal-approximation intervals understate fat-tail risk.

Verification of the nine-loss-streak remark (added so the figure is not unexplained precision). Assumptions: 120 independent trades, each a loss with probability 0.58 (the complementary 42% win rate used in this fictional report), and a streak meaning nine losses in a row anywhere in the sequence. Under those assumptions an exact recurrence (a short Markov chain that tracks the current loss run and absorbs at nine) gives probability 0.3053 of at least one nine-loss run. A Monte Carlo of 200,000 independent sequences with seed 20261107 produced 0.3051. The earlier wording about a 30% chance matches this calculation; it is not a market forecast and it is not valid if trades are dependent or the loss rate is different. A naive count of 112 overlapping windows times 0.58 to the ninth overstates the probability (about 0.83) because the windows are not independent.

The broader lesson stands: painful streaks are compatible with a modest positive expectancy. They are not, by themselves, proof that the edge died, and they are not proof that you should double size to recover.

VaR versus drawdown: the fictional 11R max drawdown is a path statistic. It can exceed any single-period VaR you compute on daily R. Do not quote VaR as if it capped that path.

modules.title: Backtesting, Bias and Validation

objectives.text: Identify look-ahead, survivorship, selection and overfitting biases
Use holdout and walk-forward testing
Correct for multiple testing
Use cost stress and counterfactual benchmarks
Decide when a paper result is credible

lessons.title: Common biases
lessons.body:
Look-ahead bias: using data not available at decision time (e.g. revised earnings, same-day close for a decision made at the open). Survivorship bias: testing only today's surviving index members ignores delisted losers. Selection/data-snooping: trying many rules and reporting the best. Overfitting: too many parameters for the data.

Why it matters: a beautiful backtest can be a bookkeeping error.

Data-quality session (core ideas you must be able to apply):

Timezone and session. A bar labelled 10:00 without a zone cannot be compared across Sydney, London and New York. If you use a US close to decide an Australian opening trade on the same calendar date, you may be using a price that has not yet happened in Sydney. Store timestamps with a time zone.

Corporate actions. A 2-for-1 split halves the raw price overnight. On unadjusted data that looks like a 50% crash and can trigger every breakdown rule you have. Use a split-adjusted series for return calculations and keep a separate corporate-action log so you can audit the adjustment. Dividends create a similar gap on price-return series; total-return series include them.

Fees and financing. Mid-to-mid backtests omit spread, brokerage, borrow and overnight financing. If the apparent edge is smaller than a conservative cost assumption, it is not an edge you have shown.

Delisting and survivorship. A universe of today's index members drops companies that failed, were acquired, or were removed earlier. Those missing names are often the losing trades. A survivorship-free study includes them up to the delist or removal date.

Missing data, stale prints and halts. Carrying the last price forward through a halt or a missing session invents zero-change returns and can create false signals. A tradable_flag of zero means do not treat this print as an executable price.

Lag versus look-ahead. Information must be available at the decision time. Using a bar's close to trade that same bar's open is look-ahead unless your written rule and fill model both say you trade the close. Future columns such as next_day_return must never be inputs to a signal.

The school's file datasets/synthetic_mini_backtest.csv is a SYNTHETIC practice series (seed 20261107, Australia/Sydney dates, no market data and no order book) built so you can see a raw split, a halt, a missing session, honest lagged signals, look-ahead signals, costs, and an in-sample versus out-of-sample split. It is not historical evidence of alpha.

lessons.title: Holdout and walk-forward
lessons.body:
Split data: develop on in-sample, then test once on untouched holdout. Walk-forward: optimise on window 1, test on next window, roll forward, and stitch out-of-sample results. Example: 10 years; train on 3, test next 1, roll yearly: 7 out-of-sample years.

Why it matters: if you look at the holdout while you develop, it is no longer a holdout.

Decision exercise: write the date you freeze development before you compute any out-of-sample number. If you then change a parameter, the holdout is contaminated and you must say so.

Walk-forward is not a magic fix: if each window secretly peeks, stitching the windows still peeks.

lessons.title: Multiple testing
lessons.body:
If you test 20 independent useless rules at 5% significance, expect about 1 'significant' by chance (20 x 0.05). Probability at least one appears significant = 1 - 0.95^20 = about 64%. Adjust thresholds (e.g. Bonferroni: 0.05/20 = 0.0025) or demand out-of-sample proof.

Why it matters: trying many ideas and reporting the winner is a selection process, even if each idea looked reasonable.

Keep a research log of how many variants you tried, including the ones you discarded. Without that count you cannot interpret a significant result. Bonferroni is a simple, conservative adjustment, not the only possible one, and it does not repair a contaminated holdout.

lessons.title: Costs and counterfactuals
lessons.body:
Re-run with doubled costs and delayed fills; if the edge vanishes, it was fragile. Counterfactuals: compare to buy-and-hold, random entries with the same exits, and the same rule on other markets. Example: strategy +8% p.a., random-entry benchmark +7.5%: edge is mostly exposure, not timing.

Why it matters: an edge that exists only at mid prices, or only against no benchmark, is usually not an edge.

Decision exercise: re-run one paper rule with doubled costs and with a one-bar delay. If the result collapses, write cost- or delay-fragile rather than promising.

lessons.title: Credibility checklist
lessons.body:
Economic rationale; few parameters; stable across nearby settings; positive out-of-sample; survives cost stress; adequate trades; documented before forward paper test. Forward paper testing is the final check before any consideration of real capital, and even then outcomes are not guaranteed.

Why it matters: credibility is a checklist, not a feeling after a good month.

Even a fully checked paper result is not evidence that you will be competent or profitable with real money. Live trading adds latency, partial fills, emotions and operational errors that a simulation does not contain.

lessons.title: Deep dive: a clean validation protocol
lessons.body:
Step 1: write the hypothesis and economic reason before looking at results. Step 2: fix the data, universe (including delisted names) and cost model. Step 3: develop on 2010-2017 (in-sample, fictional dates). Step 4: walk forward over 2018-2022 with yearly re-optimisation, recording the out-of-sample segments only. Step 5: test once on the 2023-2025 holdout; no further tuning. Step 6: run robustness checks: parameter neighbours (+/-20%), 2x costs, one-bar delayed entry, other markets, random-entry benchmark. Step 7: run a forward paper test for a pre-set number of trades (e.g. at least 50) with a pre-set stop rule. Invented illustration (not the SYNTHETIC file and not a historical study): in-sample Sharpe 1.8, walk-forward 0.6, holdout 0.4, 2x costs 0.1. Interpretation: most of the in-sample performance was fit to noise; the remaining edge is small and cost-sensitive. Invented counterfactual in the same illustration: same exits with random entries produce Sharpe 0.3, so the timing contributes little. Those Sharpe figures are teaching numbers, not out-of-sample results used to select or reject a rule after seeing the holdout, and they are not taken from datasets/synthetic_mini_backtest.csv. Common errors: peeking at the holdout repeatedly; deleting 'bad' periods; using survivorship-biased constituent lists; no record of how many variants were tried. Limitations: no protocol proves future profitability.

Worked mini-backtest (SYNTHETIC file, not a market study). Using datasets/compute_backtest.py with seed 20261107:

The generated raw series includes a 2-for-1 split. The unadjusted close-to-close return on that day is about -50.7%; the split-adjusted return is about -1.3%. That gap is exactly the corporate-action trap: a rule on raw prices can read a split as a crash.

A halt day and a missing day are flagged tradable_flag = 0. Using those rows as ordinary closes would invent a tradable print.

A long-only rule (hold when the lagged split-adjusted close is above an N-day average, fill the next open) is run for N in {5, 10, 15, 20, 30} on the first 120 rows (in-sample) with 10 basis points of cost each way. The best in-sample honest net result in this invented path is N = 15 at about +0.75%. The same N on the unused last 60 rows is about -3.97% net. Choosing N by the in-sample ranking and quoting only +0.75% would have been overfitting.

On that same in-sample window, the invalid look-ahead version (decide and fill on the same close) prints about +2.03% net for N = 15, larger than the honest figure. The extra is an artefact of using information that was not available at the open.

None of these percentages is a forecast, a claim of alpha, or a reason to trade the rule. They exist so you can re-run the script and obtain the same numbers. If your own rerun differs, you are not looking at this file or this seed.

Common additional errors: putting next-period returns into the signal file; downloading a survivorship-biased constituent list and calling it a universe; and presenting polished statistics after you already peeked. This course does not compute a deflated Sharpe statistic in this version; if you see one elsewhere, treat it as another adjustment that still cannot prove future profits.

modules.title: Disciplined Paper Practice, Ethics and Critical Thinking with AI

objectives.text: Run a structured paper trading process with journals and reviews
Apply ethics: market integrity, honesty and conflicts
Use AI tools critically and verify outputs
Plan responsible next steps without promised profits

lessons.title: Process over outcomes
lessons.body:
A trading plan lists: markets, setups, entry/exit rules, sizing, risk limits, review schedule. Journal every paper trade: thesis, evidence, plan, result, emotion, lesson. Review weekly: rule-following rate, expectancy, mistakes. Good decisions can lose; bad ones can win; judge the process across many trades.

Why it matters: a plan you have not written will not be the plan you follow after a loss.

Process, not outcome, is the grading target. A losing trade that obeyed the plan scores better than a winning trade that broke a risk rule. That is uncomfortable, and it is the point.

Human learning and AI-strategy learning are separate tracks. Completing lessons and paper journals in this school does not automatically approve an uploaded strategy, and a paper-tested uploaded strategy does not complete the school on your behalf. Keep the records apart so that neither track borrows credibility from the other.

lessons.title: Psychology and behaviour
lessons.body:
Common biases: loss aversion, overconfidence, recency, confirmation bias, revenge trading, FOMO. Counter with checklists, pre-commitment, cooling-off rules (e.g. no new trades after 3 consecutive losses in a day).

Why it matters: most broken risk rules are broken for emotional reasons that feel rational in the moment. A structured process exists to pre-commit while you are calm.

A practical psychology loop:

1. Before the session, precommitment. Write the markets you may trade, the maximum number of new paper trades, the per-trade risk, the heat cap, and the conditions that force no trading (drawdown ladder, unverified news, upcoming binary event outside the plan, or an emotional state you have named in advance such as anger after a loss).

2. During the session, a short checklist before each order: Is this a planned setup? Is the size calculated from the stop? Is the correlated group still inside its cap? Am I opening this to recover a loss? If any answer fails, the trade is a no.

3. Losing streaks are mathematically ordinary. Module 19 showed that a nine-loss run can occur about 30% of the time in a 120-trade sample with a 58% loss rate under independent-trade assumptions. A streak is information to review, not an automatic verdict that you should abandon the plan or double size.

4. Revenge is the urge to place a new trade quickly so that the loss does not count. Cooling-off rules (for example no new trade after three losses in a day, or after any critical-mistake flag) are precommitments against that urge.

5. Overconfidence is the mirror image after a winning streak: widening size because I am seeing it clearly now. Size stays at the precommitted fraction until you change the written plan in a review, not mid-session.

6. Strategic no-trading is a successful output. When a gate fails, the correct action is to stand aside. No-trade days are not laziness in this framework; they are rule-following. Journal them as such.

7. After the session, separate process marks from P&L. Ask what you would repeat if the outcome had been the opposite.

This loop does not make anyone an excellent trader and does not remove emotion. It makes emotion visible and reviewable.

lessons.title: Ethics and market integrity
lessons.body:
Never spread false information, manipulate prices (pump-and-dump, spoofing, wash trading), or trade on inside information. Disclose conflicts when discussing investments. Professional codes such as the CFA Institute Code of Ethics emphasise integrity, diligence and putting clients first. Be honest about paper vs real results.

Why it matters: skill without integrity is still harm, and in markets it can also be unlawful. This module gives general education, not legal advice and not a schedule of penalties, which vary by jurisdiction and change.

Honesty includes how you talk about paper results. Presenting simulated marks as live performance, or as proof you are a qualified trader, is a reporting failure even if no law is cited here.

lessons.title: AI critically
lessons.body:
AI assistants can summarise, calculate and generate ideas, but can be wrong, out of date, or fabricate sources. Verify facts with primary sources, check calculations, ask for assumptions, and never let an AI tool override your risk limits. AI signals in this app are paper-only educational tools, not advice.

Why it matters: fluent language is not the same as a checked fact or a safe order.

Upload Skills (teaching an AI trader) should follow the same rails as any other strategy change: you upload or describe a method; the system (or a reviewer) restates what it understood; you correct misunderstandings; the method is paper-tested with costs; it receives a version number, results and an approval status; and it must not bypass written risk limits. An uploaded prompt that says ignore the stop, increase size to recover, or this cannot lose is rejected, not tested for profit. Approval is a process state, not a certificate of excellence.

Naive trust, pasting a prompt and enabling it because the wording sounds expert, is a critical process mistake. It is different from using AI to draft a journal entry or to check arithmetic, which you still verify.

Human-school progress and AI-strategy approval remain separate records. Do not let a high quiz score stand in for an untested upload, or a lucky uploaded backtest stand in for completed coursework.

lessons.title: Next steps responsibly
lessons.body:
This course is general education, not personal financial advice and not a regulated qualification. Before real money: understand your goals, emergency fund, debts, tax and product disclosure documents; consider licensed advice. No strategy guarantees profits; losses can exceed expectations.

Why it matters: finishing a course creates a tempting story about being ready for live risk. That story is not evidence.

What completion can mean: you demonstrated a paper process against a published rubric. What it cannot mean: industry accreditation, a licence, a prediction of profit, or proof that you will execute well with real money. Simulation, including this app's paper mode, cannot by itself evidence live-trading competence.

If you later consider real money, that is a personal financial decision outside this course. This school does not instruct you to go live and does not represent that any paper result will survive contact with live markets, taxes, product rules or your own behaviour.

lessons.title: Capstone: practical assessment, journal, mistake review and rubric
lessons.body:
The capstone is assessed beyond multiple choice. Requirements: (1) a written paper trading plan; (2) at least 30 journaled paper trades (a proposed default, configurable); (3) a weekly mistake review; (4) a final report. Each journal entry records: setup, thesis, counter-evidence considered, entry, stop, target, size calculation, correlated group, event calendar check, fill vs arrival price (slippage), exit reason, rule adherence (yes/no), emotion, and lesson. Mistake taxonomy: risk (oversize, heat cap breach, correlated stacking), execution (market order in thin book, ignored spread), discipline (moved stop, revenge trade, skipped journal), analysis (ignored counter-evidence, overfit rule), integrity (misreported result). The rubric scores 0-3 per criterion (see rubric in course.json): position sizing accuracy; correlated-risk control; drawdown rule adherence; gap and event-risk planning; slippage and cost accounting; stop discipline; explaining counter-evidence; process-vs-luck analysis; overfitting avoidance; honest reporting. Pass (proposed default): average >= 2.0, with no criterion at 0, and no unremediated critical mistake. Completion means the learner demonstrated the process in paper conditions; it does not certify trading skill, predict profits or make anyone a qualified or excellent trader.

Capstone scoring, stated as a product default rather than an owner-made law. The 80% quiz pass mark, the suggestion of at least 30 journaled paper trades, the 0-3 rubric, an average at least 2.0 with no criterion at 0, and critical-mistake remediation are configurable defaults proposed for the product. They are not a regulator's standard and not an automatic certification. Changing them is a server-side configuration decision, not something a learner or an AI upload can waive in order to pass.

Critical-mistake remediation (default behaviour): if the journal or practical shows a critical breach, oversize beyond the stated multiple of planned risk, heat or correlation-cap breach, trading through a halt rule, widening a stop after entry, no exit plan on a leveraged position, holding leverage into an unplanned expiry or binary event, or misreporting results, the module is marked remediation required even if the quiz passed. The learner submits a written mistake review and one corrected paper trade (or a documented no-trade decision if the right correction was not to trade). Until that is recorded, the capstone is not a pass.

Profit is not a pass criterion. A negative expectancy over the paper sample can still pass if process, risk arithmetic and honesty meet the rubric; a profitable sample can fail if a critical mistake is unremediated or if reporting is incomplete.

Human versus AI evidence: capstone journals are evidence about the human learner's process. Uploaded-strategy paper tests are evidence about that strategy version. Neither is live-competence evidence; neither is accreditation.

No drawdown number in the plan is a guarantee. The capstone asks whether you stress-tested gaps and correlation, not whether the future obeyed your stress number.

practical_rubric.scale: 0-3 per criterion (0 absent, 1 inconsistent, 2 consistent with objective evidence, 3 consistent with clear worked evidence). Paper-only. Profit or a positive paper P&L is not a pass criterion.
practical_rubric.pass_default: Proposed configurable default: mean score at least 2.0, no criterion at 0, and no unremediated critical mistake. Self-declared profit does not pass a failed process or maths criterion.
practical_rubric.retry: If any critical process or risk-arithmetic criterion scores 0, or if a listed critical mistake appears, mark remediation required even if the quiz passed. The learner resubmits the missing objective evidence (corrected workings, journal fields, or a documented no-trade decision) before the practical can pass. Configurable product default, not an owner-made law and not accreditation.
